description: "Batch multiple loosely-related issues into one PR — the 1-review-per-hour CodeRabbit ceiling, not the work, is what sets wave throughput"
metadata:

  modified: 2026-08-08T12:45:56.750Z
---

The user is happy to batch **multiple loosely-related issues into one PR** to keep review cadence
flowing. Stated 2026-08-08 during wave 8.

**Why:** CodeRabbit gives one review per hour org-wide, so a wave of N single-issue PRs costs at
least N hours of review chain whatever order it runs in. The file-ownership graph caps how much can
run in *parallel*; the review slot caps how fast anything *lands*. Batching cuts the number of
cycles, and it is the only lever that moves the real bottleneck. See
[[project-v2-hot-file-contention-caps-parallelism]] for the other half of the constraint.

**How to apply:**

- Batch by **shared file surface first, topical relation second**. Two issues that both touch
  `facade.rs` belong together whether or not they are conceptually related, because splitting them
  guarantees a rebase. Two issues in the same subsystem that interact semantically (one changes
  where auth state comes from, the other what happens when restore fails) belong together because
  splitting them makes the second rework the first.
- 2–3 issues per PR is the working size. Do not build one giant PR: review quality drops, and
  CodeRabbit has a [[project-coderabbit-150-file-cap]].
- Give each issue its own commit inside the batch, and a `Closes #N` line per issue in the body.
- When adding scope to an agent already mid-build, tell it to finish the original issue coherently
  first and add the second on top — and to ship the first alone if the second turns out much larger
  than scoped. A blocked bug fix is worse than an extra review cycle.
- Still hold a batch behind a genuine blocker. Batching changes how work is grouped, never whether
  a dependency edge is respected.

Related: [[feedback-closes-vs-part-of-issue-hygiene]] (one `Closes` per finished issue),
[[feedback-keep-prs-draft-control-cr-timing.md]] (the orchestrator owns slot timing).

**Reaffirmed and strengthened 2026-08-19 (wave 11):** "I would like each of the PRs to close more
than one issue (if possible and appropriate)." Treat a single-issue PR as needing justification,
not as a default. This applies to slices already planned but **not yet opened** — re-batch them
mid-wave rather than waiting for the next wave.

Two things make re-batching easier than it looks mid-wave:

- A hot-file slot **frees the moment its PR merges**. The "one PR per wave per hot file" rule is
  about PRs in flight together, not the wave as a calendar unit. Once the `facade.rs` claimant
  merges, a later PR in the same wave can claim `facade.rs` — it just rebases.
- Combining is sometimes the *better review*, not merely the cheaper one. Two halves of one
  security protocol (server exchange + browser key custody) reviewed separately means no review
  ever sees the binding between them.

Related: [[project-worktree-branch-ref-goes-stale]] when re-batching into an existing branch.

An approver leaves an orphan factor behind when an approval fails after the seal.

`mintApprovalFactor` in `apps/web/src/auth/coreKit.ts` calls `createFactor` and
then `commitChanges`, so the fresh factor is on the account before the seal runs
and before the response is sent. Every failure after that point leaves a
committed device factor that opens nothing, and each retry adds one more.

The obvious repair does not work. The seal step transfers the factor bytes to
the engine worker, so `ApprovalPrompt` holds a detached buffer once
`deviceRendezvous` returns and can no longer name the factor it would delete.
Copying the bytes to keep a handle would hold live key material in the tab for
the length of the exchange, which is what the transfer exists to prevent. A
delete after the response was sent is worse still: a response the API accepted
but whose acknowledgement was lost would strand the device that was let in.

So this needs a design rather than a patch — an approver-side record of what a
rendezvous minted, or a mint that follows the accepted response and re-seals.

# Wave 19 — standing rules for every lane (read fully before any action)

You are one lane of wave 19 in FSM1/cipher-box. You work in your OWN git worktree (already created for you; run `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` and `git branch --show-current` first and use that path for everything). Your scratchpad is `/tmp/w19/lane-<lane-id>/` — create it; never write outside your worktree, that scratchpad, or GitHub.

## Setup
- `pnpm install` in the worktree (never symlink node_modules). Do not share CARGO_TARGET_DIR with any other checkout.
- Prefix EVERY `gh` call with `env -u GITHUB_TOKEN`. Write shell commands in full (zsh; variables do not word-split).
- Read `AGENTS.md`, `CONTEXT.md`, and the blueprint file(s) for your component. Use CONTEXT.md terms exactly.
- Read your rows in the recon report named in your lane brief (`/tmp/w19/report-<X>.md`) — they carry the verified file surface, the stale-body notes and the decision defaults.
- MANDATORY recon: when a feature existed in v1, read the reference implementation on branch `v1` (`git show v1:<path>`, `git ls-tree -r v1 --name-only | grep ...`) before designing.

## Issue hygiene (before coding)
- If the recon report says a body or title is stale, edit it (`env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh issue edit N --title/--body-file`) so it states the CURRENT code facts. Keep the original scope; append a dated "Body check 2026-09-14" section rather than rewriting history.
- FILING BAR: disposition order for any new finding = implement now in this PR > fold into an OPEN issue (comment) > file a new `post-cutover` issue ONLY for a real defect. Every filed issue: milestone `post-cutover`, labels `v2-build` + exactly ONE `comp:*`, a parent (sub-issue of the component umbrella: engine #1702, core #989, web #993, desktop #994, ci #995, deploy #996, api #655), and a native dependency edge both ways when it depends on / blocks something. Never write a closing keyword to negate it.
- All prose you write to GitHub (issue bodies, comments, PR body, reports) is ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English: short active sentences, simple tenses, no contractions, no idioms. Code and quoted output exempt.

## Code rules (AGENTS.md is authoritative)
- All crypto/codec in Rust (`crates/core`), engine logic in `crates/engine`; TS only in packages/client, packages/login, packages/auth-ui, apps/web, apps/desktop, tests/*. String literals over TS enums.
- Determinism injected (no direct clocks/RNG in core/engine). Zeroize at the terminal owner only.
- Encode/decode fail-closed symmetry: encode-side invariant checks are release-active `Err`, never `debug_assert!`/`assert!`; cover with a test that fires in release.
- Comments: why, not what; short; no absence-justifying comments, no unchanged-code apologia, no tracker refs (`pnpm lint:tracker-refs`). State an invariant once at its home.
- Assert behaviour, never source text.
- HeadTooLarge stays retryable. Prefer hard-delete over DB crypto. Store the narrowest derived capability. No secret material in test assertions.

## Verification before you open the PR
- Rust: `cargo fmt --all --check` (ALL, never `-p`), `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test -p <crate>` for every crate you touched. If you touched a seam trait, `crates/wasm`, or any wasm-bound type: `cargo check -p cipherbox-wasm --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` (find the exact crate name in crates/wasm/Cargo.toml) and run the packages/client suite.
- TS: `pnpm -r typecheck`, `pnpm lint`, the affected package's `pnpm test`. If a wasm-bound class or client type changed, run the `apps/web` vitest suite (typecheck cannot catch stale fixtures). Web vitest runs `*.test.ts` only.
- `pnpm lint:tracker-refs`, `pnpm lint:md` if you touched markdown (delete `target/doc` first if you ran cargo doc).
- Rebuild `packages/client` dist before a consumer typecheck.

## Review gates — run INLINE as checklists (do NOT spawn nested review sub-agents; they stall)
1. simplify pass over `git diff main...HEAD`: remove speculative generality, dead abstraction, duplication, long comments.
2. security pass: trust boundaries, fail-closed, auth/expiry, injection, DoS/resource exhaustion, concurrency, determinism seams.
3. crypto-privacy pass whenever the diff touches crates/core primitives, key/seal material, or a trust-boundary read.
Fold real findings into code + tests before opening the PR. Write a 5-line summary of each pass into your scratchpad `review.md` and quote it in your final report.

## Git / PR
- Never push to main. Branch name is given in your lane brief. One commit per issue when practical, Conventional Commits, no parentheses in the subject, no `Closes` in commit messages (it leaks into the squash message).
- Commit signing goes through 1Password and can hang: wrap `git commit` in `timeout 120`; if it hangs, retry once; never use `--no-gpg-sign`. Verify with `git log -1` — do not trust the helper's exit code alone.
- Before pushing, `git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main` (a bot release commit may have landed).
- Open the PR as a DRAFT: title = Conventional Commit, no parens; body with a bare `Closes #N.` line per finished issue (not backticked), a "Body checks / follow-ups filed" section, and NO tool attribution of any kind (no "Generated with", no Co-Authored-By). Escape only non-issue `#NN` text. Verify the rendered body.
- Wait for CI with ONE foreground polling script (sandbox refuses bare `sleep` loops longer than the call; use `timeout 540000` on the Bash call and poll every 60 s inside a script). Known flaky REQUIRED checks — re-run once before triaging: Web E2E Smoke, Windows link.exe 1104, Desktop Build matrix.
- DO NOT request a CodeRabbit review, DO NOT mark the PR ready, DO NOT merge. The orchestrator owns the review slot chain and will resume you by message for `/resolve-pr-reviews` if findings arrive.

## Final report (your last message; the orchestrator reads only this)
PR number + branch + head sha; CI status per check; issues closed by the PR; body/title edits made; follow-ups filed (numbers) or folded (issue + comment link); the three inline review summaries; anything left undone and why. STE-100 prose.

2026-09-14T00:08:30Z
----
Part of #995. Motivated by #1818.

## Why

The v2.0.2 deploy shipped two defects that only a real browser against the real staging front can show: a CORS preflight allow list on the routing vhost, and a cacheable "not found" answer from someguy (#1818). No suite drives a browser through the Caddy front today. The Tag Staging Release workflow runs the Web E2E and Desktop E2E suites on the local CI stack before it tags, and the deploy job has no post-deploy gate. The blueprint names a staging-dispatch job with real login (`blueprint/testing.md`, staging release gates) that does not exist yet.

The v1 e2e regimen on branch `v1` ran real-world usage profiles against staging. This issue copies that intent onto the v2 web app.

## Scope

A staging e2e suite in `tests/web-e2e`, run by a dispatchable workflow, and chained after the deploy job in the Tag Staging Release workflow. It drives Chromium at `https://app-staging.cipherbox.cc` and reaches the API, the routing front, and the gateway through Cloudflare. A red run blocks nothing on merge, but the workflow result is the release verdict for the staging tag.

### Harness changes

1. A `staging` Playwright project. When `E2E_BASE_URL` is set, the config skips both local web servers and uses that URL. The v1 config did the same with `BASE_URL` (`tests/web-e2e/playwright.config.ts` on `v1`).
2. A login path for a hookless bundle. `shipsE2eHook` in `apps/web/src/engine/config.ts` refuses the introspection hook on every deployed build, so the suite must use a shipped method: an injected test wallet for the SIWE method, or a browser entry backed by the `TEST_LOGIN_SECRET` that the staging deploy already writes. Decide this first; it gates every profile below.
3. Test accounts and cleanup. Each run uses fresh identities and removes what it created. Staging rate limits need a bypass for the run, as v1 used the `X-Throttle-Bypass` header on staging only (`tests/TESTING_STRATEGY.md` on `v1`).
4. Fixture media as real files: an image, a PDF, an audio file, a small video, a large video, as in `tests/web-e2e/fixtures/files` on `v1`.

### Usage profiles

Each profile is one spec. The list copies the v1 journeys; the third column names what is new on staging.

| Profile | Steps | Staging adds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First login and vault mint | Log in with a fresh identity, wait for the vault, reload, sign out, sign in again | Real login round trip, the root-record publish through the routing front, session survival across the front |
| Workspace build | Build a 6-folder tree, upload files into each folder, rename, move by menu and by drag, delete, and read the tree back after a reload | Real someguy publish latency and the drain against the real name store |
| Size matrix | Upload 100 B, 1 KB, 5 KB, 10 KB, 50 KB, 100 KB, 250 KB, 500 KB, and read each back byte for byte | Real Kubo ingest and real gateway reads through Cloudflare |
| Batch operations | Multi-select with click, shift, and select-all, then batch delete, batch move, batch download | Concurrent publishes on the real name store |
| Recycle bin | Delete, restore, purge, empty, retention, quota reclaim | Real unpin and real reclaim |
| Sharing and revoke | Owner grants a folder to a second account, adds a file after the grant, revokes, and the recipient loses access | Second real account, real grant propagation, a cut visible through the CDN |
| Writable share | Recipient uploads, creates subfolders to depth 2, renames, deletes; owner reads back; downgrade to read-only and back | Two real sessions on one scope through one front |
| Invite link | Mint for a file and a folder, unauthenticated landing, claim, browse, revoke, and the error matrix | Real claim route behind Caddy and Cloudflare |
| Second device | Device approval approve and deny across two browser contexts; recovery-phrase restore on a second browser | Real rendezvous transport and real expiry windows |
| Media | Preview an image and a PDF; stream a small and a large video | Real range requests through Caddy and Cloudflare |
| Offline queue | Go offline in the browser, queue uploads and folder ops, reconnect, and confirm the drain | A real reconnect against the staging API |
| Journey timing | Record login-to-vault, upload-to-visible, and share-to-accessible against a committed baseline, as in `tests/web-e2e/baselines/staging-journey-timing.json` on `v1` | The only environment where these numbers mean anything |

Load, spike, sustained, and the BYO capacity ladder stay in `crates/load` and are out of scope here.

### Workflow

- `staging-e2e.yml`: `workflow_dispatch` with a base URL input that defaults to the staging app, and `workflow_call`. It builds nothing; it runs the `staging` project against the live URL and uploads the Playwright report and the timing JSON as artifacts.
- `tag-staging.yml`: call `staging-e2e.yml` after the deploy job. The deploy has no health gate today, so this run is also the first signal that the containers came up.

## Acceptance

- A dispatch of `staging-e2e.yml` against the current staging runs every profile above and passes.
- The suite fails red when the routing front preflight omits `Content-Type`, or when a "not found" answer reaches the browser with a cache lifetime. Prove this once against a deliberately broken front, or with a request interceptor in the test, and record the result in the PR.
- The Tag Staging Release run shows the staging e2e result after the deploy.
- Every suite blocks a merge in a named gate the day it lands (`blueprint/testing.md` law 1): the staging project itself cannot block a PR, so the harness changes must keep the local `e2e` and `release` projects green in the existing gates, and the blueprint suite map gains the new job.

**Decisions applied**
- #1806 and #959 postponed, no wave 19 lanes. #831 moves to wave 20. #1792 waits for your Windows session.
- #1778 takes option 1, push-to-main. #1094 follows the v1 behavior, with mandatory v1 recon, at the wave tail.

# usage: wait-until.sh <HH:MM UTC>
target=$(date -u -j -f "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M" "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%d) $1" +%s)
now=$(date -u +%s)

  left=$((target-$(date -u +%s))); [ $left -gt 500 ] && left=500
  sleep $left
  [ $(( $(date -u +%s) )) -ge $target ] && break
done

The issue body placed the "keep only while the endpoint and the kind are unchanged" rule in the web form alone. CodeRabbit asked me to store the cached record's sequence, hold the cached copy to the current floors, reject it when it fails them, and degrade when the metadata cannot be read.

**Rejected.** Three reasons, each checked against the code:
- **Not introduced here.** On `main`, `load_settings_at` already returned `SettingsLoad::Stale` from the cached block for every degraded reason, with no floor comparison (`git show f8ab9cce7~1:crates/engine/src/settings.rs`, lines 927-935). The comment sitting above them on `main` states the rule and cites `blueprint/engine.md`: a rollback takes this arm like every other reason, because pinning last-known-good is what the record plane owes a gate failure.
- **A merge-blocking test asserts the opposite of the request.** `a_stale_copy_decides_placement_like_a_resolved_record` in `crates/engine/src/settings.rs:1344` requires a stale copy to decide placement exactly as a resolved record does, and cites `blueprint/engine.md` "Settings-load policy". The requested change would fail it.
- **The premise is wrong.** There is no unauthenticated cache metadata to distrust. The cache holds one value, the sealed head block, and the seal open authenticates it. Storing a plaintext sequence beside it would *create* the unauthenticated metadata the finding warns against; sealing one would be a wire-format change. Containment already exists: `BinIndexLoad::writable` returns `Err` for every `Stale`, so a cached copy can never be published over.

### Finding 2 — rebase the adopted revision on a sequence advance (Minor, `record_plane.rs:365`)

**Rejected.** Also unchanged by this branch — `resolve_settings` and `resolve_bin_index` both ended with the same two independent monotonic advances on `main`. On reachability: `floor::mint_revision` (`crates/engine/src/gate/floor.rs:413`) mints `max(mint_floor, adopted_floor) + 1`, so a device never mints a revision at or below its own adopted bar, and publishing at a higher sequence requires first adopting the live record. A lower revision at a higher sequence therefore does not arise from a device that followed the publish path. The residual is the lost floor write, whose refusal `DefaultsReason::StrandedMint` documents as deliberate. Critically, the proposed rebase would *lower* the adopted bar — a revision floor that can move down is not a floor, and it would re-open the same-sequence replay window the bar exists to close. Applying it would be a security regression.

engine: carry one queue hold with a reason rather than three parallel hold cells

Part of #992

`comp:engine` · **M** · `crates/engine/src/sync/drain.rs`, `crates/engine/src/facade.rs`, `crates/wasm/src/lib.rs`

Found by the simplify, reuse and altitude gates on PR #1658.

## Problem

The drain holds the queue head for three reasons, and each has its own cell: `BlockedOp` for the quota, `SettingsHold` for a placement refusal, and `BinIndexHold` for a bin index the pass cannot read. All three carry the same three fields — `op_id`, `node`, one reason payload — and all three are mutually exclusive. Nothing makes the exclusion structural. Each halt arm clears the other cells by hand, and the invariant lives only in a comment:

> One pass raises one halt, and each hold's own gate is what lets go of it — so taking one drops the others rather than leaving two cells claiming the same head for different reasons.

PR #1658 added the third cell and six such clear calls. A fourth reason makes it twelve, and a missed clear leaves two cells that name one head.

## Scope

Replace the three cells with one `QueueHold { op_id, node, reason }`, where the reason is `Quota { needed_bytes }`, `Settings(SettingsRefusal)` or `BinIndex(DefaultsReason)`. One pre-pass gate dispatches on the reason, so the per-arm clears go away and exclusion holds by construction.

The change is mechanical but wide: about 74 references across `drain.rs`, `facade.rs`, `crates/wasm/src/lib.rs`, `crates/engine/tests/write_plane.rs`, `crates/wasm/tests/boundary.rs` and the desktop tests. It replaces three public `SnapshotView` and `SessionStatus` fields and three wasm-bound classes, so it touches the TypeScript-facing surface.

## AC

- [ ] The drain holds one cell, and taking a hold cannot leave a stale one behind.
- [ ] No halt arm clears another arm's state by hand.
- [ ] The host reads the same information it reads today, through one field.

PR #1642 turns one drain pass per tick into one pass per proved scope root. Four pieces of per-tick bookkeeping were written for a session that held exactly one scope. None of them is a trust boundary and none is attacker-reachable, but each now means something slightly different from what its own comment says.

## The holds are now per pass, not per tick

`apply_valve` in `crates/engine/src/sync/drain.rs` clears the bin-index hold on the first halt that is not a bin read, and `drain_queue` clears the block hold, the settings hold and the bin-index hold whenever its own view of the queue is empty. With one pass per scope, an unclassified halt in scope B drops a hold scope A took in the same tick. Each hold's own pre-pass gate re-takes it on the next tick, so the surface recovers, but the hold is no longer the per-tick statement its doc block makes it.

## `MAX_BIN_EXPIRIES` is now a per-scope bound

`expire_bin_entries` runs once per scope, so a tick can stage up to `MAX_BIN_EXPIRIES` purge ops per proved scope rather than per tick. The passes do not duplicate each other, because each admits only entries whose `scopeId` is its own, and the scope count is owner-controlled rather than attacker-controlled. The frozen "a bounded share per pass" intent is still multiplied by the scope count and should either be restated or re-bounded per tick.

## The walk's label map is not charged against the attempt bound

`bind_child_labels` runs per frontier level before the attempt budget is consulted, so the label map grows with the total index size across levels rather than with the number of descents the walk pays for. Reaching the worst case needs a large number of genuinely gate-passing owner scope roots, so it is not attacker-reachable. Charging the label bind against `MAX_SCOPE_DESCENT_ATTEMPTS` closes it cheaply.

## The proved-set clear at session switch is best effort

`Engine` clears `descendant_scope_roots` with `try_borrow_mut` and skips silently when the cell is borrowed, matching the seed maps above it. That set now decides the own-plane floor namespace in `floor_view`, so a stale entry surviving a session switch would give a new account's grafted scope the owner floor plane on a 128-bit scope id collision. The probability is negligible; the failure mode is now a trust-boundary one rather than bookkeeping, so the clear should be unconditional or its failure should be surfaced.


## From the second crypto pass, on the fold itself

### The walk cannot tell an empty index from a refused write plane

`ScopeWalk::descendant_scope_roots` calls `write_plane` for its own index read and takes `(None, vec![])` on a refusal, which is the same answer as "this vault holds no descendant scope". The facade then runs `install_descendant_scopes` with an empty proved set, which drops the read and write seeds of every promotion it already knew, so each one's focus leg serves nothing until a later tick re-proves it.

The eviction path is not new: any `write_plane_of` failure already produced an empty index. The seed check added for the critical finding widens the set of triggers by one. The direction is right — fail closed, self healing, availability rather than a trust verdict — and it is not a new denial-of-service lever, because only a party who can already publish a gate-passing record at the vault root's own name can set the offending owner-write-blob, and that party can deny the plane outright.

The fix is availability only: have `write_plane` distinguish "no seed, or a seed that does not name us" from "the index is empty", and have `descendant_scope_roots` answer `None` in the first case so the facade keeps last-known-good seeds.

engine: the move-replace vacate reclaims nothing under the folder it frees

## Problem

A delete owes reclamation. `publish_delete` in `crates/engine/src/sync/drain.rs` walks the doomed subtree, retires every registry name in it, and unpins the content it held.

A vacate is also a delete — #1522 made the model say so, and `Snapshot::relocate` now takes the replaced node's whole subtree. The publish plane did not follow. `publish_ref_move` drops one child ref for the vacated node and owes nothing for what sat under it.

So a move that replaces a non-empty folder leaves every descendant's registry name live and its content pinned, with no parent ref left anywhere that a later walk could reach them from. Nothing can reclaim them after the fact.

## Why it is latent, not live

`crates/fuse/src/ops.rs` refuses to replace a folder that holds anything except platform junk, and it queues real delete ops for that junk first. So today the vacated subtree is always empty by the time the move publishes, and the leak never fires. The model and the publish plane sit at different depths, and only one caller's discipline hides it.

## Scope

Pick one depth and state it there:

- either the vacate owes the same reclamation a delete owes, and `publish_ref_move` walks the vacated subtree the way `publish_delete` walks a deleted one,
- or the "a vacate only ever frees an empty folder" rule moves out of the mount and into the facade, where `Replaced` is formed, so every host inherits it.

The first is the honest one if `Command::Move { replacing }` keeps its current freedom. The second is cheaper and narrows the facade surface.

## AC sketch

- A move that replaces a folder with descendants either reclaims them or is refused before it publishes, and the choice is stated where `Replaced` is formed.
- No path leaves a registry name live for a node no parent ref reaches.
- The rule holds for any host, not only for the FUSE mount.

Surfaced by the altitude pass on the #1522 fix. Part of #991.

## The finding
One actionable comment, Major, on `crates/engine/src/sync/drain.rs`: a head held over the account quota keeps that hold when the placement is `Err`, because `quota_admits` returned `false` without asking the quota endpoint. The member then reads "over quota" while the real cause is their own settings.

**Verified as real, but the proposed diff was wrong.** CodeRabbit suggested `if self.placement.is_err() { self.release_hold(); }`. Tracing the mechanism: `upload_version` maps an `Err` placement through `PlacementRefusal::holds`, which returns `Some` for `NoProvider` and `NoExternalIngress` but `None` for `SettingsUnavailable`. A `holds` refusal reaches `Halt::HeldBySettings` and charges nothing; `SettingsUnavailable` reaches `Halt::Unclassified`, which charges `charge_unattributed` and dead-letters the op with `AttemptsExhausted` at `UNATTRIBUTED_BUDGET`, which is 120 passes. A blanket release therefore turns an op waiting on an unreadable settings record into a dead letter the member must recover. I also confirmed the behaviour is not new in this PR: the identical early return stood in `quota_admits_the_held_head` before the refactor.

## What I changed
Accepted in substance, rejected as written. `quota_admits` now returns `settings_refusal(self.placement).is_some()` on an `Err` placement. A settings refusal is a verdict, so the hold goes and the next pass re-takes the hold its own rule names; an outage is not a verdict, so the head stays held and spends no budget. This also matches the rule the neighbouring comment already states for a placement with no hosted leg. Regression test `a_quota_hold_lets_go_of_a_refusing_placement_and_waits_out_an_undecided_one` asserts both arms through `hold_admits_the_head`; I confirmed it fails against the previous `return false` before restoring the fix.

visible and online. The gate is only visibility, network state and the account factor policy.

2026-09-03T23:16:48Z
An approver leaves an orphan factor behind when an approval fails after the seal.

`mintApprovalFactor` in `apps/web/src/auth/coreKit.ts` calls `createFactor` and
then `commitChanges`, so the fresh factor is on the account before the seal runs
and before the response is sent. Every failure after that point leaves a
committed device factor that opens nothing, and each retry adds one more.

The obvious repair does not work. The seal step transfers the factor bytes to
the engine worker, so `ApprovalPrompt` holds a detached buffer once
`deviceRendezvous` returns and can no longer name the factor it would delete.
Copying the bytes to keep a handle would hold live key material in the tab for
the length of the exchange, which is what the transfer exists to prevent. A
delete after the response was sent is worse still: a response the API accepted
but whose acknowledgement was lost would strand the device that was let in.

So this needs a design rather than a patch — an approver-side record of what a
rendezvous minted, or a mint that follows the accepted response and re-seals.
Raised while closing FSM1/cipher-box#1695, whose flag split does not reach it.

On a failure before the API accepted the response, delete that factor by its identifier. On a failure after the API accepted the response (an acknowledgement lost), keep it: deleting would strand the device that was let in. engine: revival corroboration is inert when the fan-out is silent and admits an at-floor content rollback [OPEN]
Two residuals the `/security-review` and `/crypto-privacy-review` of #703 raised
that its fix deliberately does not reach. Both are bounded to the user's own
past states — no forgery — but both leave revival trusting less than it could.

## 1. The fan-out cannot distinguish "no endpoint answered" from "no endpoint has it"

`net::fanout::fanout_get_verify` swallows every per-endpoint transport error as
`continue` and returns `None`, which is byte-identical to "the endpoint set
answered and nobody serves this name". `net::revival::revive` therefore falls
back to a recovery-endpoint-only basis in both cases. An attacker who controls
the recovery endpoint and is on-path for the routing set gets exactly the
pre-#703 behaviour: replay an old owner-signed record and have the device
re-mint its superseded CID at a fresh higher sequence.

The device's durable sequence floor is the second gate, but it defaults to 0 on
a name the device has no floor for — which is the common case after the >EOL
lapse revival exists to recover from.

Fix direction: give `fanout_get_verify` a return shape that separates "answered,
no record" from "nobody answered", and refuse a recovery-only basis when zero
endpoints answered. That return type is consumed by `resolve`, `publish`,
`settings`, `rotation` and `pointer_fetch`, so it is a wider change than #703's
slice.

## 2. A basis exactly at the durable floor is admitted with any content

`revive` admits `basis.sequence >= floor`. Consider: this device durably adopted
sequence 5; another device rotated and published sequence 6; sequence 6 is gone
from every endpoint after the lapse. Both sources yield sequence 5, the check
passes, and revival re-mints the pre-rotation CID at sequence 6 — superseding
the rotation cut with pre-revocation content. Gated readers then reject the new
head on the epoch stage, so this degrades into a fail-closed lockout at that
name rather than an accepted rollback.

Fix direction: at `basis.sequence == floor`, require the basis to be the record
the device actually adopted — either by retaining the adopted head value
alongside the sequence floor, or by threading the scope id in and putting the
basis envelope through the adoption gate before it becomes the re-mint head.
Both add durable state or a new dependency to the revival slice.

## Scope note

`net::revival::revive` has no production caller yet, so neither residual is live.
They should be closed before revival is wired into the liveness loop.

---

## Body check 2026-09-14

The code facts below replace the ones this body states above. The scope is unchanged.

- Residual 1 is now a call-site change in `net::revival::revive`, not the repo-wide
  return-shape change the "Fix direction" paragraph describes.
  `net::fanout::fanout_get_classified` and its `FanoutRecord` return type already
  exist. They separate `Absent` — every endpoint answered, and every answer was
  "no record" — from `Unavailable`, which is silence. `net::liveness` is the first
  consumer. `fanout_get_verify` stays as the collapsing wrapper for the callers
  that want it, so `resolve`, `publish`, `settings`, `rotation` and
  `pointer_fetch` are not touched.

engine: a scope boundary the session has not proved reads as no boundary, and the overlay reaches it [OPEN]
## The gap

`classify_crossing` resolves a relocation's two ends against `relocation_scope_roots()`, which is the union of `minted_scope_roots` and `descendant_scope_roots`. Both sets are in-memory and session-scoped, and both are cleared at teardown. `descendant_scope_roots` is written only by `install_descendant_scopes`, which the tick calls after `ScopeWalk::descendant_scope_roots` proves a level.

Before the first successful descent walk the set is empty. `scope_of` then answers the render root for both ends of every move, so a relocation that truly leaves a granted scope classifies as `ScopeCrossing::Intra`.

The `classify_crossing` doc already accepts this: a boundary the session has not proved reads as no boundary. What the doc does not say is that the pending-op overlay reaches it.

## Why the overlay reaches it

`apply_overlay` handles `OpKind::Create` and `OpKind::Restore` with an unconditional `view.link_next(*parent, op.target)`, and `Snapshot::link_next` does not require the parent to exist in the base. So a durable queued create whose parent is a granted scope root places the new node under that root in the render at cold start, before the walk runs.

`parent_of` then answers `Some(scope_root)`, so the placement refusal does not fire, and `classify_crossing` answers `Intra` for a move out of that scope.

## What it costs today

The publish does not happen. The drain re-checks the boundary in `ensure_folder`, which `publish_ref_move` calls for both ends, and its `scope.scope_roots` is rebuilt from the session set on each pass:

- If the walk has since succeeded, `halt_below_another_scope_root` stops the pass.
- If the walk is still failing, `load_child_folder` attempts the granted folder under the vault-root seed, the unseal fails, and the pass halts.

So the cost is a mis-journaled op the caller was already told succeeded, plus — in the second sub-case — an availability failure that surfaces as an abuse report. That is the "availability laundered into a trust verdict" shape `install_descendant_scopes` warns about, and security rule 6 names.

## What to decide

The residual is a scope-boundary read, so the choice belongs in the decision corpus and then in `CONTEXT.md`, because it changes what an offline client may journal.

Two candidates:

- Make the proved descendant scope roots durable per account, so a cold session starts with the boundaries the last session proved. This narrows the window to a first run only.
- Refuse a relocation whose either end sits under a scope root this session has not re-proved. Note that refusing every relocation until a walk lands is not acceptable on its own: metadata ops queue unbounded offline (blueprint/engine.md "Sync core: Ops"), so an offline session must still be able to move a node inside one scope.

## Acceptance

- The chosen rule is stated in `CONTEXT.md` and in `blueprint/engine.md`.
- A test drives a session with a durable queued create under a granted scope root, before any successful descent walk, and asserts the chosen verdict for a move out of that scope.
- The accepted-residual paragraph on `classify_crossing` is corrected or removed, because it currently understates the reach.

Found by the `/crypto-privacy-review` and `/simplify` passes on #1651.

## What

A write grant runs the write-scope cut after it publishes the grantee scope root and updates the parent index. PR for #1549 moved the share-pointer post past that cut, so a failed cut now leaves a scope the recipient never learns of, rather than a grant they hold and cannot use. The residual stays: no command re-drives the owed wave.

## Evidence

`crates/engine/src/facade.rs` `share_scope` calls `cut_granted_write_scope` after `create_grant`, and `post_share_pointer` after the cut. A cut that fails returns the error to the owner. The scope root is published and the parent index names it, so `record_share_standing` reports `AlreadyAScope` and refuses a re-share of the same folder. The owner must revoke the grantee and grant again.

## Scope

Option 1 of #1549: make the cut resumable. A granted scope root whose write epoch is still the one it inherited, and which no scope pointer names, is a detectable unfinished state. Drive the owed wave from a start-up reconciliation pass, or admit a re-share of exactly that folder.

## Acceptance

- A write grant whose cut fails once completes on a later owner session, with no revoke in between.
- A test drives a failing cut, then a successful re-drive, and asserts the moved root and the grantee's re-minted blob.

## Body check 2026-09-14

The contact-grant arm landed in PR #1777. The invite-link arm is now landed too, for the session that minted the link: `share_scope` holds the `PendingInviteLink` its mint produced, and a re-drive of `CreateInviteLink` at the same node proves the published root commits exactly the row that link's own throwaway invitee mints, then runs the owed wave and seals the fragment at the moved name. `resumable_write_share` now takes the recipient key pair, so one rule serves both share kinds.

What is still open here:

- **A resume across sessions or devices.** The durable invite record keeps only the invitee public halves, because the invitee secret is the whole bearer capability. Nothing can rebuild a `PendingInviteLink` from the record. A device that did not run the stalled mint therefore refuses, and the revoke stays the remedy there. To close this, the owner must keep the invitee secret durably, which is a privacy decision about the staging store rather than a defect fix.
- **A start-up reconciliation pass.** Still a design question, as the 2026-09-06 comment states. It is not needed to remove the member-visible outcome on the contact path or on the link path inside one session.

The first acceptance line ("completes on a later owner session") is therefore met for a contact grant and not met for an invite link.

content.text:
Noted on v2.0.3. Staging now carries the front fix, so the staging profiles in #1831 can go green when its slot comes.

Four decisions wait on you. Each one is a rule choice, not a bug fix, so a lane cannot take it alone. My recommendation comes first in each list.

## 1. #1161 part 2: revival at the floor

**The situation.** Revival recovers a name after its record lapsed from every endpoint. Part 1 landed: revival now refuses when no endpoint answered at all. Part 2 is open: revival accepts a basis whose sequence equals the device's own durable floor, with any content. If another device rotated at sequence 6 and that record is gone, both sources give sequence 5, and revival re-mints the pre-rotation content at sequence 6. Readers then reject that head at the epoch stage, so the outcome is a lockout at that name, not an accepted rollback. Revival has no production caller yet, so nothing is live.

**Options:**

- **A. Keep the adopted head beside the floor (recommended).** The device stores the head value it last adopted, next to the sequence floor it already stores. At the floor, revival accepts only that exact record. Cost: one more durable value per name in the floor store, no wire-format change. Benefit: the lockout case cannot arise.
- **B. Put the basis through the adoption gate.** Revival threads the scope id in and gates the basis envelope before it becomes the re-mint head. Cost: a new dependency from revival into the adoption gate. Benefit: same as A, with no new durable state, but more code on a trust path.
- **C. Defer until revival is wired.** Leave part 2 open and re-visit when revival gets its caller in the liveness loop.

## 2. #1735: an unproved scope boundary at journal time

**The situation.** A fresh session has not yet proved which folders are scope roots. A move that leaves a granted scope can be journaled as a move inside one scope. The drain re-derives the crossing from the planes it proves, so the published result is correct either way. The doc and a test that proves this landed in wave 19. What stays open is the rule.

**Options:**

- **A. Record the rule as it stands (recommended).** The journaled crossing is a plan, and the drain is the authority. Cost: none. This is what ships today. The queued op's crossing field can be wrong for a moment that no member and no attacker can observe.
- **B. Durable proved scope roots per account.** A session starts with the boundaries the last session proved. Cost: new per-account durable state, readable from a second device, a stale entry becomes a boundary the session believes without proof, and an ADR. Only worth it if a later change makes the journaled crossing authoritative somewhere.

A separate residual on the same gap: the tick groups file children of an unproved scope root onto the enclosing scope, and those rows report an honest writer as abuse. That is not a decision, only work. I can add it to the next lane on the focus path.

## 3. #1601: resume a stalled invite link from another device

**The situation.** A write share through an invite link runs the write-scope cut after it publishes the root. If the cut fails, the session that minted the link can now re-drive it. A different device cannot, because the durable invite record keeps only the public halves of the invitee key. The invitee secret is the whole bearer capability, so nothing can rebuild the pending link elsewhere. The remedy there is revoke and share again.

**Options:**

- **A. Accept the residual (recommended).** Same-session resume is landed. Cross-device resume is a revoke and re-share. Close #1601 with that recorded. Cost: none.
- **B. Keep the invitee secret in the owner's durable store.** Then any owner device can re-drive. Cost: a bearer capability at rest in the staging store, encrypted under the owner's key, for as long as the link stays unfinished. This is a privacy posture change and needs an ADR.
- **C. A start-up reconciliation pass.** A pass that detects a granted root whose write epoch is still inherited and no pointer names, and runs the owed wave. It does not help the link case without B, because it still needs the invitee secret.

## 4. #1722: does a probe raise the cut-epoch floor

**The situation.** A probe gates a scope root without committing the gate pass. It drops two floor advances: the name's sequence floor, which is the point of the probe, and the scope's cut-epoch floor, which is the restrictive one. The cut-epoch floor makes a device refuse an old grant set that a revoked recipient replays. Every path that keeps the probed root goes on to a real adopt, which raises both. Only a foreign genesis root keeps nothing, and its cut epoch stays unrecorded until the next resolve of that scope.

**Options:**

- **A. A probe spends nothing (recommended).** Record at the trait definition that a probe is a sighting, and test that it advances neither floor. Cost: a foreign root's cut-epoch floor waits for the next resolve. This is what the code does today and keeps one durable write path on the adoption gate.
- **B. Split the commit.** Let a probe write the cut-epoch raise alone. Cost: a second durable write path on the adoption gate. Benefit: the foreign root case raises the restrictive floor one resolve earlier.

If you take the four recommendations, three are documentation plus a test, and only #1161 A adds a small durable value. I can batch those into one engine lane.

content.text:
Here is each decision again, in plainer words and with the costs from the code.

## #1161: revival at the floor

**What revival is.** Every folder record lives on the IPFS network under a name. Records expire. If a device comes back after a long absence and finds that the network lost the record for a name, revival re-publishes the last copy the device can find, at a higher sequence number. Two guards protect that re-publish. First, the device only accepts a copy from the network if at least one endpoint answered. That guard landed in this wave. Second, the device keeps a floor per name: the highest sequence number it ever accepted. It refuses any copy with a lower number.

**The gap.** The floor check is "at or above". So a copy with exactly the floor number passes, even if it is not the same record the device accepted before. Example: this device accepted version 5. Another device rotated the folder key and published version 6. Version 6 then lapsed from the network. The revival now finds a version 5 from the recovery endpoint, and republishes it as version 7. That version 7 carries the old key generation, so every reader rejects it. The folder becomes unreadable at that name. Not a data leak, but a lockout.

**Option A, keep the accepted record beside the floor.** The floor store is a small durable key-value store on each device: a file store on desktop, IndexedDB in the browser. Today it holds one number per name and one number per scope. Option A adds one value per name: the identity of the record the device accepted, about 40 bytes. Storage cost is nothing that matters. The development cost is a seam change: one new method on the floor store trait, and four implementations to update, the desktop store, the browser bridge, the client TypeScript store, and the test fake. Plus the write must join the existing batched floor raise so it cannot land half. About one medium lane.

**Option B, gate the copy through the adoption gate.** Revival is 142 lines with no production caller yet. Option B makes revival open the found copy with the device's own keys and run it through the same checks a normal read runs, before it becomes the new head. No new storage and no seam change. Cost is that revival grows a dependency on the adoption gate and needs the scope id and the read seed threaded in. About one small-to-medium lane, all inside the engine crate. The gate check is the stronger check, because it checks the content and not only the identity.

**My take.** B is cheaper and stronger. I recommended A earlier because it keeps revival independent. On the costs, B wins.

## #1735: an unproved shared-folder boundary at start

**What a scope root is.** A folder you shared is a scope. It has its own keys, separate from the vault's. Its top folder is the scope root. Moving a file out of a shared folder is not a plain move: the file must be re-encrypted under the vault keys, and the shared folder must get a key cut so the recipient loses reach. Moving a file inside one folder tree is a plain move.

**The gap.** When the app starts, it does not yet know which folders are scope roots. It learns that from a walk over the network, which can take a while or fail offline. Until then the app treats every folder as inside the vault. If you move a file out of a shared folder in that moment, the app writes the move into its offline queue with the note "plain move".

**Why it does not matter today.** The publisher, which is the part that later pushes the queue to the network, does not trust that note. It re-checks the boundary against what it has proved by then, and does the re-encryption and the cut. This wave landed a test that drives exactly this and proves the published result is right. So the wrong note is a note no one reads.

**Option A, write that rule down.** State in the blueprint and in the code that the queue note is a plan and the publisher is the authority. Zero cost. That is the code today.

**Option B, remember the scope roots across restarts.** The app saves the list of proved scope roots per account and loads it at start, so the first moves already know the boundaries. Cost: new durable per-account data, a second device must be able to read it, and a stale entry becomes a boundary the app believes without proof. That is a trust posture change and would need an ADR. It buys nothing today, because the publisher already gets it right.

**My take.** A. Take B only if some later feature starts to trust the queue note.

## #1601: an invite link whose last step failed

**What an invite link does.** You share a folder with write access to someone you have no contact for, through a link. The link carries a secret the recipient needs. Sharing runs four steps: publish the folder as a scope root under new keys, add it to the parent listing, cut the write key so the folder gets its own write key, then publish the pointer the link resolves to.

**When it manifests.** Step three fails, for example the network drops. Now the folder is marked as a scope in your parent listing, but the link does not work yet. If you try to share the same folder again, the app refuses with "already a scope". Before this wave, the only way out was revoke and share again. This wave fixed it for the same session: the device that made the link still holds the link's secret in memory, so it can retry the cut and finish.

**What is still open.** A different device, or the same device after a restart, cannot finish it. The link's secret is the whole bearer capability. The durable invite record stores only the public half, on purpose. Without the secret, nothing can rebuild the pending link. So on another device the remedy stays revoke and share again.

**Option A, accept that.** Close the issue with the rule recorded. Zero cost. The failure is rare, it needs a network drop inside one share, and the remedy is one revoke.

**Option B, store the link secret on the owner's device.** Then any of your devices could finish the share. Cost: a bearer secret at rest in the local store, encrypted under your key, for as long as the share stays unfinished. That is a privacy posture change and needs an ADR. Also a small engine lane.

**My take.** A.

## #1722: a probe and the cut-epoch floor

**What a probe is.** A normal read of a scope root record does two things: it checks the record, signature, epoch, and so on, and then it adopts it, which records it as the current head and raises two floors on the device. A probe does only the first half. It looks at the record and checks it, but adopts nothing. The engine uses a probe at vault creation, to see whether a root already exists at the name before it mints one.

**The two floors.** The sequence floor says "I never accept an older version of this record". The cut-epoch floor says "I never accept a key generation older than this for this scope". The second one is what stops a revoked recipient from replaying an old grant set.

**The gap.** The probe raises neither floor. That is the point for the sequence floor. For the cut-epoch floor it is a small loss: the device learns the key generation a little later, at the first normal read of that scope. Every path that keeps the probed root goes on to a normal read anyway. The only path that keeps nothing is a probe of a root that belongs to someone else at vault creation.

**Option A, a probe spends nothing.** Record the rule at the trait, add a test that proves a probe raises neither floor. Zero engine cost. That is the code today.

**Option B, split the adopt.** Let a probe raise the cut-epoch floor alone. Cost: a second durable write path on the adoption gate, the most trust-critical code in the engine, for a window that is one read wide and only on the someone-else's-root case.

**My take.** A.

If you agree with B for #1161 and A for the other three, I can batch all four into one engine lane: one code change with a test for #1161, and doc plus test for each of the rest.

Your reasoning holds for the network. Every record carries its own expiry, signed at publish. Version 6 was published later than version 5, so its expiry is later. An honest routing node drops version 5 before it drops version 6. So a copy of version 5 cannot come from the honest network once version 6 lapsed.

The copy in the scenario comes from the recovery endpoint. That is the API's record cache, a database row, so it never expires. The API's republisher refreshes that row from the network on a 12-hour cadence and refuses a sequence that goes backwards. Version 6 stays visible for its whole 90-day validity. For the API to still hold version 5, version 6 must have stayed invisible to the republisher for 90 days. In a working system that does not happen.

So the case reduces to an attacker. The attacker must control the API's recovery endpoint and sit on the network path of this device, and replay version 5 on both. Part 1, which landed this wave, already refuses when the network path is silent. Part 2 covers the case where the attacker answers on both with a valid old record at exactly the floor. The outcome is that this device republishes its own old content at a new sequence, and every reader then refuses that head at the key-generation check. That is a lockout of one name, caused by an attacker who controls both the API and the network path. That attacker can already deny the name outright. The content is content this device itself accepted before, so nothing leaks.

Two more facts change the weight:

- **Revival has no production caller.** Nothing in the liveness loop calls it yet. Until that lands, neither residual is live.
- **The at-floor case needs this device to have missed version 6 entirely.** If it ever saw version 6, its floor is 6 and version 5 is refused today.

**My revised take.** Part 2 buys a refusal instead of a lockout, against an adversary who can already cause a lockout. That is not worth a seam change, and not worth a new dependency in revival either. I recommend a new option:

- **C. Record the residual and close.** State on the revival module doc that a basis at the floor is admitted, why the honest network cannot produce a stale one, and that the attacker case is denial only. Close #1161 with that recorded. When revival gets its production caller, that issue re-reads the residual, and the choice between A and B can be made then with a real caller in front of it.

If you prefer to keep a tracker hook, the alternative is to leave #1161 open as a blocker of the issue that wires revival into the liveness loop, with no work now. I can check whether that wiring issue exists.

=== 1094
engine: retain prior file versions and expose restore and delete [v2-build,comp:engine]
Version history is v2 scope, but **v2 currently has no version concept to surface**. There is no `VersionEntry`, no `restore`/`delete` version command, and no prior-version field anywhere in `crates/engine`, `crates/core`, or `packages/client`. This issue is the engine half; the web surface is tracked separately.

## Why this is not a port

v1 kept a `VersionEntry[]` per file and let the UI download, restore, or delete a past version. v2's content model actively works against that as built:

- Each version is **fresh-keyed** — the content key is random per version and stored inline in that version's sealed read-body (`CONTEXT.md`). A prior version therefore remains openable only while its own read-body is retained.
- **Orphan GC** reclaims staged roots nothing references. A superseded content root has no referent once the node advances, so prior versions are not merely unsurfaced — they are collectable.

So retaining history is a retention and reference-counting decision in the engine, not a rendering gap.

## Scope

- Decide and document the retention rule: how many prior versions a node keeps, and what makes their content roots referenced so orphan GC leaves them alone.
- Expose prior versions on the node in the snapshot — at minimum an identifier, a size, and a timestamp per entry.
- Facade commands to **download**, **restore**, and **delete** a specific prior version.
- Restore must go through the normal write path so it publishes as a new version rather than mutating history.
- Update `CONTEXT.md` with the term, and `blueprint/engine.md` with the retention rule and its interaction with orphan GC.

## Tests

- A superseded content root survives orphan GC while it is within the retention rule, and is collected once it falls outside it.
- Restoring a prior version publishes a new version whose content matches the restored one.
- Deleting a prior version makes it unresolvable and its bytes collectable.
- A version retained across a key-regression epoch still opens.


---

## Correction 2026-08-18 — verified at `7d3f93fb1`

**"v2 currently has no version concept" is no longer true.** At `main`:

- `ReadBody::File` already carries a `versions: Vec<Version>` list.
- `plan_prune`, `keep_latest` and `RetentionPolicy` already live in `crates/engine/src/content/retention.rs` (751).

### 1. Add a deadline to each fetch attempt — ACCEPTED, fixed

I verified the mechanism before acting, and CodeRabbit's framing needed one correction. Node *does* bound the connect phase: an unreachable host rejects after 10 s with `ConnectTimeoutError`, which I had already seen earlier in this lane. It does **not** bound the response body. I stood up a local server that answers `200`, writes a partial JSON body and never ends it:

- unguarded `fetch` + `response.json()` — still pending after 6 s
- same call with `AbortSignal.timeout(2000)` — rejected at 2007 ms with `TimeoutError`

So the stall is real, and it is the body read rather than the connect. The job's `timeout-minutes: 5` means it is not literally unbounded, but the retry loop never runs and the operator sees a killed job instead of the readable `Could not read <source>` message.

I did not apply the suggestion literally. The budget is **15 s** per attempt, not CodeRabbit's 30 s, so three attempts plus the two 5 s delays reach 55 s worst case and stay well inside the job's own 5-minute cap. The observation is factually correct but the resulting failure is not actionable. I ran three cases through the real script against a local server:

- **A** exact 22 ranges → exit 0

- **C** a duplicate **and** one range removed → exit 1, still naming `- 173.245.48.0/20 (trusted, no longer published)`

feat: retain prior file versions and expose restore and delete
Closes #1094.

File versions behave as they did in CipherBox v1. The engine half lands here; the web dialog is #1095.

## v1 behaviour, and what v2 does

Read from branch `v1`.

| Question | v1 behaviour | v1 reference | v2 in this PR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| How many versions are kept | The `maxVersionsPerFile` vault setting. Default `10`, clamped to `0..=100`. `0` turns versioning off. | `packages/core/src/vault/settings.ts:18,47`; `packages/sdk-core/src/file/index.ts:29` | The `keepLatestVersions` vault setting drives `RetentionPolicy::KeepLatest`. The default before the member chooses is `10`, the same number. |
| What one entry carries | `cid`, `fileKeyEncrypted`, `fileIv`, `size`, `timestamp`, `encryptionMode`. Every field from the sealed per-file metadata record. | `packages/core/src/file/types.ts:10-25` | `contentCid`, `size`, `modifiedAt`. Every field from the sealed read-body. The per-version content key stays inside the engine. |
| How a version is named | By its index into the array. There is no id. | `apps/web/src/services/file-metadata.service.ts:386` | By its `contentCid`. A history carries no other identifier, and an index moves under a concurrent write. |
| What restore does | The current content becomes the newest entry and the restored entry leaves the list. The bytes are re-referenced, never re-uploaded. History keeps its length. | `apps/web/src/services/file-metadata.service.ts:403-409` | The same. The restore publishes a new record whose head is the named version, with the outgoing head as the newest prior version. No byte moves. |
| What delete does | The entry leaves the list, the current content is untouched, the record republishes, and the removed CID is unpinned. | `apps/web/src/services/file-metadata.service.ts:449-459` | The same, through the retire ledger, which names every block of the version. |
| Can the current version be deleted | No. The list holds prior versions only, so the current version has no row and the SDK has no call for it. | `apps/web/src/components/file-browser/details/FileDetails.tsx:98-107` | Refused, at the command and again at the drain. |
| Order, and is the current version listed | Newest first. The current version is not in the list. | `packages/core/src/file/types.ts:47` | The same. |
| Per-version actions | Download, restore, delete. | `apps/web/src/components/file-browser/details/VersionHistory.tsx` | Download, restore, delete. |

### Where the v2 model forces a difference

1. **No version cooldown.** v1 had a `versionCooldownMinutes` window, default `15`, in which a re-upload overwrote without making a version. v2 refuses a clock in this decision because the op queue must replay deterministically, which is the reason the owner already declined an age-based retention rule. Every content write therefore makes a version.
2. **A delete is final.** Each v2 version is fresh-keyed and its key rides inside the file's sealed read-body, so a retained version opens only while its entry is retained. Dropping the entry leaves the bytes addressed but no key to open them. v1's unpin was best-effort and left the key in the record.
3. **Retire, not unpin.** v1 unpinned a single CID from the web tier and logged a warning on failure. v2 journals what the drop owes to the retire ledger before the shortened history publishes, so a crash cannot lose the debt.
4. **An explicit `0` is not representable.** v1 allowed `maxVersionsPerFile: 0` to turn versioning off. `RetentionPolicy::KeepLatest` takes a `NonZeroU64`, because keeping zero would plan the retire of the live version along with its history. A member who wants no history deletes the versions.

## What changed

**Retention.** The rule is enforced where history grows: `publish_update_content` shortens the list it is about to seal. A vault therefore never carries a version past the rule, not even between a write and a prune. `publish_prune` now goes through the same `shorten_history` helper, so the plan, the repeated-CID refusal and the debt journal have one home. Every retained version's root is re-registered under the file's own name on each publish, which is what keeps orphan GC off it.

Shortening history retires bytes and cannot be undone, so the drain acts only on a settings load that carried a member choice. A device that could not read the settings record keeps every version, which is the rule the bin's expiry sweep already follows.

**Reads.** `Engine::file_versions` lists the prior versions off the file's own record through the same gated child pipeline `read_content` uses, and `Engine::read_version_content` opens one under its own key. Neither is a snapshot field: a history is per file and unbounded by the folder render, and a host asks for it when it opens a file's details.

**Commands.** `Command::RestoreVersion` and `Command::DeleteVersion` stage `OpKind::RestoreVersion` and `OpKind::DeleteVersion`, each naming its target by `contentCid`. A restore is a rotate of the sealed list, so no version's content key is moved out of the list that owns it. A delete removes the entry, which zeroizes its key.

**Boundary.** A `VersionEntry` class, `fileVersions`, `downloadVersion`, `restoreVersion` and `deleteVersion` are bound in `crates/wasm` and mirrored in `packages/client`, so the web lane has a surface.

**Docs.** `CONTEXT.md` gains the **Version history** term. `blueprint/engine.md` states the retention rule, the referenced-equals-kept interaction with orphan GC, the member-choice condition, and the restore-is-a-write law. The old "keep all versions within quota" line is replaced.

## Review gates

**`/simplify`** — one `shorten_history` and one `journal_retire_debt` replace what `publish_prune` held alone; one `open_file_record` for the two new drain paths; a control-flag parameter became `version_position` returning the index. A shared helper for the `publish_node` tail was considered and rejected: four call sites already carry that argument list, so the helper would need seven parameters and would reach into untouched code.

**`/security-review`** — one real finding, fixed. The automatic retention could return a permanent refusal on a history whose `contentCid` repeats. A version list is authored by anyone holding the scope's write seed, so a co-writer could have parked every later write to that file. A history this build refuses to shorten now publishes whole, covered by a test. Also checked: the member-choice condition above, fail-closed dead-lettering of a version the record no longer names, the gated resolve behind both new reads, and that no clock enters retention, restore or delete.

**`/crypto-privacy-review`** — `VersionEntry` carries no key material and none crosses the WASM boundary. A restore reuses the existing version's own key and re-encrypts nothing, so fresh-keying is preserved. A delete drops the entry, which zeroizes its `SecretBytes`. The plaintext a version download returns is wiped at the boundary like `download`. Every version's key rides in the one read-body, so the lazy-wave re-seal carries the whole history across a cut; covered by a test. No test asserts on key material.

## Tests

Each one fails on the unfixed code.

- `a_content_write_retires_only_the_version_the_retention_rule_drops` — a superseded root inside the rule is retained, and the write that pushes it outside the rule is the one that retires it.
- `a_content_write_with_no_member_retention_choice_keeps_every_version`
- `a_write_over_a_history_retention_cannot_shorten_still_publishes`
- `restoring_a_prior_version_publishes_it_as_the_new_head_and_keeps_the_history`
- `deleting_one_version_makes_it_unresolvable_and_retires_its_blocks`
- `a_delete_of_the_current_version_is_refused`
- `a_version_retained_across_a_key_regression_epoch_still_opens`

- #1094 — a dated "Body check 2026-09-15" section was appended. You are one lane of wave 19 in FSM1/cipher-box. Never write a closing keyword to negate it.
- All prose you write to GitHub (issue bodies, comments, PR body, reports) is ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English: short active sentences, simple tenses, no contractions, no idioms. Code and quoted output exempt.

## Code rules (AGENTS.md is authoritative)
- All crypto/codec in Rust (`crates/core`), engine logic in `crates/engine`; TS only in packages/client, packages/login, packages/auth-ui, apps/web, apps/desktop, tests/*. String literals over TS enums.
- Determinism injected (no direct clocks/RNG in core/engine). Zeroize at the terminal owner only.
- Encode/decode fail-closed symmetry: encode-side invariant checks are release-active `Err`, never `debug_assert!`/`assert!`; cover with a test that fires in release.
- Comments: why, not what; short; no absence-justifying comments, no unchanged-code apologia, no tracker refs (`pnpm lint:tracker-refs`). State an invariant once at its home.

## Verification before you open the PR
- Rust: `cargo fmt --all --check` (ALL, never `-p`), `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test -p <crate>` for every crate you touched. 1. simplify pass over `git diff main...HEAD`: remove speculative generality, dead abstraction, duplication, long comments.
2. security pass: trust boundaries, fail-closed, auth/expiry, injection, DoS/resource exhaustion, concurrency, determinism seams.

PR number + branch + head sha; CI status per check; issues closed by the PR; body/title edits made; follow-ups filed (numbers) or folded (issue + comment link); the three inline review summaries; anything left undone and why. STE-100 prose.

## What happens

On the deployed staging front, a folder grant does not reach the recipient.

The owner grants a folder to a second identity through the share dialog. The dialog re-reads and shows the grant row with the recipient identity key and the permission, so the command was accepted and published. The recipient's `/shared` stays on `// nothing has been shared with you yet`.

Measured on 2026-09-16 against `https://app-staging.cipherbox.cc`, three consecutive runs: the recipient polled for 10 minutes, clicking the status indicator and then `shared-reload` every 5 seconds, so every turn forced a no-cache sync pass and then re-read the list. No row ever appeared, and the footer stayed on `syncing...`.

## What was ruled out

- The contact import: the owner's picker listed the recipient, and the grant row carries the recipient identity key.
- A stale read on the recipient: the poll re-reads the list on every turn.
- A missing sync pass on the recipient: the poll forces one on every turn.
- The account: both identities are fresh, and both are deleted at the end of the run.

## Why it matters

Sharing is unusable on the deployed front. The owner sees a grant that stands, and the recipient sees nothing, with no refusal on either side.

## Where to look

The delivery leg between the grant publish and `ShareInbox::pull` on the recipient: the mailbox message, and whether the recipient's forced pass reaches the inbox at all.

## How it was found

The staging sharing and writable-share profiles. Both are held out of the run while this stands; both name this condition as their skip reason, and both run again as soon as it clears.

ci: cover file bytes, size, mtime and a second session in the cross-client suite
v2-build,comp:ci
## Problem

The cross-client suite (`tests/cross-client`) writes only folders. Every scenario creates or deletes a folder at one host and lists its name at the other. No scenario writes a file, asserts a size or an mtime, restarts a host, or logs in a second time onto a vault that already has content.

The smoke tests of 2026-09-05 found four defects in exactly those paths, and the suite was green for all of them:

- a file another device adds paints no size until the folder is re-entered (#1779, #855, #1800)
- a mount that starts a new session lists no children under a sub-folder (#1783)

The README already records the second gap as a known limit: a tab that cold-starts onto a vault a mount already published does not converge, and `offline-convergence` works around it by holding the tab up across the outage. A limit a suite works around is a path the suite does not test.

## Scenarios to add

### `file-round-trip`

1. The mount writes a file with known bytes into a folder.
2. The tab lists the file with the same name, the same size and an mtime inside the write window, on the nocache passes the CI timing profile allows.
3. The tab uploads a file into the same folder.
4. The mount lists it with the same name and size, and reads back the same bytes.

The tab-side assertion must read the rendered size and mtime cells, not only the name. A row that shows `...` for size must fail the scenario.

### `second-session`

1. The mount creates a folder and a file inside it. The tab creates a second file inside the same folder.
2. The desktop instance quits.
3. A fresh desktop instance starts on the same secret and mounts.
4. A directory listing of the sub-folder returns both children, with their sizes, on one nocache pass.
5. A fresh tab opens on the same secret and lists the same children.

Step 5 is the cold-start convergence the README lists as a limit. If it still does not converge, the scenario must fail and name the engine defect rather than work around it.

## Notes

- The `desktop-e2e` scenario `write-round-trip` already reads file bytes back on one mount, so the byte helpers exist. The tab side needs a size and mtime reader in the files page object.
- Both scenarios ride the desktop mounted matrix and report under `Cross-Client E2E (<platform>)`, the same as the five scenarios there now.
- Blocked on the harness consolidation the shared e2e helpers issue tracks, if that lands first; otherwise land on the current helpers and let the consolidation carry them.

I was not aware of the failed run before you asked. I read it, and I read #1872. The failure is not a one-time event.

**What failed.** The nightly job Cross-Client E2E on macOS failed in the scenario `second-session`, which PR #1871 added. The first mount did not show the file that the tab uploaded within the 30 second wait. The other six scenarios passed, and Linux and Windows passed.

**It fails on every main run.** Three main runs since #1871 merged all failed in the same scenario:

| run | trigger | failed step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 35181867749 | push to main after #1871 | a fresh tab listed 0 rows at the root in 30 s |
| 35211355950 | nightly, filed #1872 | the mount did not show the tab's file in 30 s |
| 35281835180 | push to main for the release | the same as the nightly |

Both dispatch runs on the PR branch passed on the same code, so the PR gate did not catch it. Both failed steps are cross-device waits with the short 30 second budget. The other scenarios use the long budget for such waits. The macOS FUSE-T SMB cache is a known second cause for a stale mount listing.

**What I did.** I launched one Opus lane in a new worktree for #1872. The lane must find the mechanism from the host logs of the three runs before it changes code. If the cause is the harness, it fixes the wait and proves it with two green macOS dispatch runs before it opens a draft PR. If the cause is the engine, it stops and reports. It does not request a CodeRabbit review. I own that slot, which is free now.

**The release.** Release v2.1.0 is tagged, the GitHub Release exists, and the desktop installers build now. Staging does not deploy on the tag. The staging deploy needs a manual dispatch of the tag-staging workflow, which then runs the assertion, the e2e gates, and the approval step. Tell me to dispatch it, or dispatch it yourself. One risk: the e2e gate in that pipeline may include the failed macOS cross-client job. I check that when the lane reports.
So the fix for #1872 is purely a CI timeout update?

Not known yet. That is why the lane must find the mechanism before it edits code.

What the evidence says now:

- **The budget is one candidate.** Both failed steps wait 30 seconds for a cross-device event. Other scenarios wait 100 seconds for such events and pass.
- **The SMB cache is a second candidate.** On macOS, FUSE-T serves a directory listing from the SMB client cache, and a new read can stay stale for over a minute. A longer wait does not fix that alone. A `stat` of the child path is a lookup and may reach FUSE where `readdir` does not.
- **An engine defect is a third candidate.** The scenario `file-round-trip` does the same tab upload and the same mount wait, and it passes every time. So the short budget alone does not explain the difference. The desktop host logs in the run artifacts show whether the engine saw the tab's publish inside the 30 seconds.

If the logs show the engine saw the publish in time, the fix is in the harness: a longer wait with a refresh per pass, or a `stat` poll. If the logs show the engine did not see it, the lane stops and reports, and the fix is an engine issue for wave 20.

  resolve-main:
    name: Resolve main SHA
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    outputs:
      sha: ${{ steps.main.outputs.sha }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          ref: main
          fetch-depth: 0
          persist-credentials: false
      - id: main
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
          # One product tag, `vX.Y.Z` (blueprint/deploy.md). The assertion is
          # anchored semver rather than a bare `v` prefix because the repo also
          # carries `v1-freeze`, which ships nothing.
          if ! git tag --points-at "$SHA" | grep -qE '^v[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$'; then
            echo "::error::No vX.Y.Z release tag on main HEAD (${SHA:0:7}). Wait for release-please to merge before tagging staging."
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "sha=$SHA" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

  # The whole suite, not the PR smoke slice `web-e2e.yml` defaults to.
  web-e2e:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - name: Calculate staging tag
        id: tag
        env:
          MAIN_SHA: ${{ needs.resolve-main.outputs.sha }}
          DESCRIPTION: ${{ inputs.description }}
        run: |
          DATE=$(date -u +%Y%m%d)
          STAGING_PREFIX="staging-${DATE}-release"
          # Find existing tags for today and get the highest release number
          LAST_N=$(git tag -l "${STAGING_PREFIX}-*" | sed "s/${STAGING_PREFIX}-//" | grep -E '^[0-9]+$' | sort -n | tail -1)
          if [ -z "$LAST_N" ]; then
            NEXT_N=1
          else
            NEXT_N=$((LAST_N + 1))
          fi
          STAGING_TAG="${STAGING_PREFIX}-${NEXT_N}"
          echo "staging_tag=${STAGING_TAG}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "## Staging Tag" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          echo "Creating **${STAGING_TAG}** from main at ${MAIN_SHA:0:7}" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          if [ -n "$DESCRIPTION" ]; then
            echo "" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
            printf 'Description: %s\n' "$DESCRIPTION" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          fi
      - name: Create and push staging tag
        env:
          STAGING_TAG: ${{ steps.tag.outputs.staging_tag }}
          MAIN_SHA: ${{ needs.resolve-main.outputs.sha }}
        run: |
          git tag "${STAGING_TAG}" "${MAIN_SHA}"
          git push origin "${STAGING_TAG}"
