41:- **Cut epoch** — the counter inside the grant-set commitment that the owner steps at every cut of a scope's grant set, and at nothing else. The adoption gate refuses any commitment below the newest cut epoch that scope already adopted, so a committed write grantee cannot restore a pre-cut set by republishing the root, and a device learns the boundary from the record rather than only from its own memory of the cut.
43:- **Structure signature** — the rotator's detached pseudonym signature over a seed-bearing structure's ciphertext and context `{scope, epoch, structure tag, recipient tag}`, carried by grant blobs, the owner blob, the owner write blob, ascent and history links, and the write-body. A missing or invalid signature is a whole-record trust violation at the adoption gate.
49:- **Floor law** — floors advance only on an AAD-confirmed unseal and cold-seed from the re-point object's owner-vouched epochs, never from a raw blob field; a grant blob's epoch field is an advisory routing hint. One exception, and the list of them is closed: the cut epoch of a grant-set commitment that passed the adoption gate's stage 2 whole raises that scope's cut-epoch floor with no unseal, under the sharer-scoped key. The owner signs that field and the signed preimage names the scope root it is presented under, so it is not a claim the network authored.
74:- **Adoption gate** — the trust pipeline every resolved record passes before adoption: signature verify, commitment verify, structure signatures against committed write pseudonyms (scope roots), strictly-newer sequence vs floor, epoch at or above the scope floor, unseal success. A failure is a fail-closed trust violation, never mere staleness.

Yes, I saw the new failure, and it changes the picture.

**The fix in #1873 did not fix main.** The run after the merge failed the same scenario again, now after the long 100 second wait. The mount did not adopt the tab's record in that time. The pattern is now clear and strange:

| trigger | runs | second-session on macOS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| push to main | 4 | 4 failed |
| workflow_dispatch on a branch | 4 | 4 passed |

Same tree, same runner image, same restored caches. So the difference is in the event or the ref, not in the code that #1873 changed. I dispatched the e2e matrix on main itself as a control run. If it passes, the event is the difference. A second Opus lane now waits for that control run, then finds the mechanism from the two job logs and the artifacts. It does not patch the engine on a hunch. If the cause is an engine defect, it stops and reports.

**You are right about the release.** The staging workflow resolves main HEAD and refuses to run without a `vX.Y.Z` tag on it. My merge of #1873 moved HEAD past the v2.1.0 tag, and a `test` commit does not make release-please cut a release. That was my error: after a release merge, nothing must merge before the staging dispatch. I saved that rule to memory. The way out is that the real fix PR merges with a `Release-As: 2.1.1` footer in the squash body. Release-please then opens the 2.1.1 PR, you merge it, and you dispatch the staging deploy at once. The staging pipeline also runs the desktop e2e gate, which includes this macOS job, so the deploy is blocked until the real fix lands in any case.

**On "adopt a record".** No, it is not the link between a node and an inode. Adoption is the engine step in the blueprint: the engine resolves the IPNS record of a scope, passes it through the adoption gate, and takes it as the current head of that folder. The filesystem projection reads the adopted state afterwards. When I wrote that the mount had not adopted the tab's record, I meant that the record existed in the record store and the mount's engine had not yet taken it as the folder's head. The inode listing was stale because of that, not because of a stale link.

## What happens

On the deployed staging front, a folder grant does not reach the recipient.

The owner grants a folder to a second identity through the share dialog. The dialog re-reads and shows the grant row with the recipient identity key and the permission, so the command was accepted and published. The recipient's `/shared` stays on `// nothing has been shared with you yet`.

Measured on 2026-09-16 against `https://app-staging.cipherbox.cc`, three consecutive runs: the recipient polled for 10 minutes, clicking the status indicator and then `shared-reload` every 5 seconds, so every turn forced a no-cache sync pass and then re-read the list. No row ever appeared, and the footer stayed on `syncing...`.

## What was ruled out

- The contact import: the owner's picker listed the recipient, and the grant row carries the recipient identity key.
- A stale read on the recipient: the poll re-reads the list on every turn.
- A missing sync pass on the recipient: the poll forces one on every turn.
- The account: both identities are fresh, and both are deleted at the end of the run.

## Why it matters

Sharing is unusable on the deployed front. The owner sees a grant that stands, and the recipient sees nothing, with no refusal on either side.

## Where to look

The delivery leg between the grant publish and `ShareInbox::pull` on the recipient: the mailbox message, and whether the recipient's forced pass reaches the inbox at all.

## How it was found

The staging sharing and writable-share profiles. Both are held out of the run while this stands; both name this condition as their skip reason, and both run again as soon as it clears.

The staging e2e job ended with 15 passed, 2 skipped and 1 failed. The 2 skipped tests are the sharing profiles that wait for #1870.

**The failure.** The assertion "the front landed every record publish" failed. Three record PUTs to `routing-staging.cipherbox.cc` ended with `net::ERR_ABORTED`. Each PUT had a different IPNS name. All three occurred less than 16 s after the sign-in and the folder create.

- a timeout or a cancel in the API client of the engine
- a worker or tab that stops
- a preflight that the browser refuses

The other staging tests keep their folders after a reload, so some publishes land. The open question is which aborted publishes the engine does not try again. The grant flake on main showed the same error on a routing GET. So this can be the mechanism of #1870, or it can be a second defect.

**#1870 is not an engine, API, front or deploy defect. It is a defect in the staging profile.**

I reproduced it on `https://app-staging.cipherbox.cc` (v2.1.1, after deploy run 35328126513 finished) with two fresh wallet identities and full network traces on both contexts. Both accounts were deleted by the fixture on every run.

Trace evidence, before the change:
- Owner `POST /mailbox/messages` → `201`, id `e84ed8ca-61e5-405c-8cc2-977c0e09caba`, at t+139 s.
- Recipient `GET /mailbox/messages` → `200` at t+141 s carrying that exact id, and on all 115 further polls through t+737 s (the full 10-minute wait).
- Recipient never sent `DELETE /mailbox/messages/<id>` and **never resolved a single IPNS name it had not itself published** — so the pass stopped before `fanout_get_verify`.

The only silent `continue` before that resolve is the sender filter in `crates/engine/src/grants/inbox.rs`: an item whose sender the recipient's own contact book does not anchor is dropped with no event and no ack. The staging profile exchanged contact codes in one direction only (recipient's code → owner). Confirmed by re-running with a two-way exchange: the recipient's `/shared` row reached standing `granted` and the recipient opened the shared folder, on both a read grant and a write grant.

**Ruled out:** the routing front (every record PUT answered `200` on both endpoints in my runs), a cached vacancy, the adoption gate, the mailbox transport and the API.

## PR
**#1889** — https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/pull/1889
Branch `fix/1876-external-unmount-acked-write`, head `36d725ff1d26a1b22b5376a221a070ffdd2bd492`. Draft. `Closes #1876` registers (`closingIssuesReferences` = [1876]). No tool attribution in the body or in the commit (`grep -ci 'co-authored\|generated with'` over `origin/main..HEAD` prints 0).

**CI: 39 of 39 checks pass, 0 fail, 0 pending.** CodeRabbit was not requested (it reports "Review skipped: draft pull request").

## Mechanism and the fix
`Projection::detach` released the mount and the operation core together. A write the mount acked and the kernel had not flushed died there with its spill: no `updateContent` op, no error on any path. `blueprint/desktop.md` "Lifecycle" says an acked-but-unpublished op is journaled and drains on the next mount, so the detach path did not do what the blueprint says the mount owes.

- `detach` now only drops the mount, so the wake stays free of an await and `next` stays cancel-safe.
- `Projection::quiesce_detached` journals every dirty handle, then releases the handles and cached plaintext. The session loop awaits it in the body of the `Ended` arm, outside the select, so the select carries no network leg and no kernel call waits behind the journal.
- The bounded journal is one function (`journal_acked_writes`) that both teardown paths call, so the five-second budget is stated once. The orderly teardown keeps its order. The journal stays separate from the kernel invalidation, which is the wedge the first shape of #1875 hit.
- Test: `crates/fuse/tests/fuse_op_core.rs` — a teardown journals every dirty handle, not the first one only.

Files: `apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/mount/projected.rs`, `apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/engine/mod.rs`, `crates/fuse/tests/fuse_op_core.rs`.

## Why no e2e scenario, and the log evidence
I wrote a desktop e2e `external-unmount` scenario and probed it on two dispatched Desktop E2E runs. Neither host it can run on proves the journal, so the scenario is not in the PR.

- **macOS: the external unmount never reaches the app.** `diskutil unmount force` reported success, then the session answered `{"mount":{"state":"mounted",...}}` on 194 reads over 20 s. Run **35359338272**, job `Desktop E2E (macos)`. The FUSE-T server keeps its fuse session open after the SMB client disconnects, so `next_op` never ends. The detach path is therefore unreachable on macOS today — which is why I could not reproduce the loss locally on FUSE-T either.
- **Linux: the scenario is vacuous.** `fusermount3 -u` does end the session, but the kernel flushes on `close(2)` first. A throwaway branch carrying the scenario and **not** the fix passed the Linux leg (run **35359527854**). Holding a descriptor open to keep the handle dirty makes the unmount refuse with `EBUSY`, so that shape does not work either. The throwaway branch is deleted.

## Follow-up filed
**#1890** — "fix(desktop): an external unmount on macOS is never reported to the app". `post-cutover`, labels `v2-build` + `comp:desktop`, sub-issue of #994, with the run link and the 194-read evidence. No body or title edit was needed on #1876; it states the current code facts.

## Review passes (from `/tmp/w19/lane-G5/review.md`)
- **Simplify:** the bounded journal is stated once and both teardown paths call it; `detach` keeps only the state the wake needs; no new type, trait or unused option.
- **Security:** trust boundaries unchanged; a failed journal still leaves its handle dirty and its spill unopenable; bounded by the five-second budget so it cannot wedge the session loop; runs outside the select, with no kernel call behind it; the only clock is the host timeout the teardown already used.
- **Crypto and privacy:** no `crates/core` primitive, no key derivation, no wire format, no trust-boundary read. The spill key stays per handle and in memory. No secret material in logs or assertions.

## Left undone
No local FUSE-T reproduction: the macOS detach path does not fire, as #1890 records. I started no local mount and no desktop process, so nothing is left running; the shared docker stack is untouched.</result>

## The gap

`classify_crossing` resolves a relocation's two ends against `relocation_scope_roots()`, which is the union of `minted_scope_roots` and `descendant_scope_roots`. Both sets are in-memory and session-scoped, and both are cleared at teardown. `descendant_scope_roots` is written only by `install_descendant_scopes`, which the tick calls after `ScopeWalk::descendant_scope_roots` proves a level.

Before the first successful descent walk the set is empty. `scope_of` then answers the render root for both ends of every move, so a relocation that truly leaves a granted scope classifies as `ScopeCrossing::Intra`.

The `classify_crossing` doc already accepts this: a boundary the session has not proved reads as no boundary. What the doc does not say is that the pending-op overlay reaches it.

## Why the overlay reaches it

`apply_overlay` handles `OpKind::Create` and `OpKind::Restore` with an unconditional `view.link_next(*parent, op.target)`, and `Snapshot::link_next` does not require the parent to exist in the base. So a durable queued create whose parent is a granted scope root places the new node under that root in the render at cold start, before the walk runs.

`parent_of` then answers `Some(scope_root)`, so the placement refusal does not fire, and `classify_crossing` answers `Intra` for a move out of that scope.

## What it costs today

The publish does not happen. The drain re-checks the boundary in `ensure_folder`, which `publish_ref_move` calls for both ends, and its `scope.scope_roots` is rebuilt from the session set on each pass:

- If the walk has since succeeded, `halt_below_another_scope_root` stops the pass.
- If the walk is still failing, `load_child_folder` attempts the granted folder under the vault-root seed, the unseal fails, and the pass halts.

So the cost is a mis-journaled op the caller was already told succeeded, plus — in the second sub-case — an availability failure that surfaces as an abuse report. That is the "availability laundered into a trust verdict" shape `install_descendant_scopes` warns about, and security rule 6 names.

## What to decide

The residual is a scope-boundary read, so the choice belongs in the decision corpus and then in `CONTEXT.md`, because it changes what an offline client may journal.

Two candidates:

- Make the proved descendant scope roots durable per account, so a cold session starts with the boundaries the last session proved. This narrows the window to a first run only.
- Refuse a relocation whose either end sits under a scope root this session has not re-proved. Note that refusing every relocation until a walk lands is not acceptable on its own: metadata ops queue unbounded offline (blueprint/engine.md "Sync core: Ops"), so an offline session must still be able to move a node inside one scope.

## Acceptance

- The chosen rule is stated in `CONTEXT.md` and in `blueprint/engine.md`.
- A test drives a session with a durable queued create under a granted scope root, before any successful descent walk, and asserts the chosen verdict for a move out of that scope.
- The accepted-residual paragraph on `classify_crossing` is corrected or removed, because it currently understates the reach.

Found by the `/crypto-privacy-review` and `/simplify` passes on #1651.

PRs #1672, #1679, #1743 and #1755 changed the cost.

What holds on main:

- The gap is unchanged. `classify_crossing` still resolves both ends against
  `relocation_scope_roots()`, which is in-memory and cleared at teardown, so a
  session that has run no boundary walk names no boundary below the render root.
- The overlay still reaches it. `apply_overlay` links a queued `Create` or
  `Restore` under a parent the base does not hold, so a durable queued create
  renders under a granted scope root at cold start.

What the cost really is:

- The drain does not use the journaled crossing. `publish_ref_move` derives

A write grant runs the write-scope cut after it publishes the grantee scope root and updates the parent index. The owner must revoke the grantee and grant again.

## Scope

Option 1 of #1549: make the cut resumable. A granted scope root whose write epoch is still the one it inherited, and which no scope pointer names, is a detectable unfinished state. Drive the owed wave from a start-up reconciliation pass, or admit a re-share of exactly that folder.

=== 1722
`Adopter::probe_read_scope_seed` gates a root without committing the gate pass. It drops the whole `PendingAdoption`, so it drops two floor advances, not one: the name's sequence floor and the scope's cut-epoch floor.

Dropping the sequence advance is the point of the probe. The mint's confirm-by-adopt step used to advance that floor and then discard the record, which left every later resolve an equal-floor `Current` that projects nothing and caches nothing.

The cut-epoch floor is different. It is restrictive: a higher value makes this device refuse a pre-cut grant set that a revoked recipient replays. Before #1641 the genesis probe called `adopt`, which raised it. Now it raises nothing.

## Why this is a hardening item and not a defect

- The raise is monotonic and idempotent.
- Every path that keeps the probed root goes on to a real adopt. `facade.rs` routes the `MovedOn` verdict into cold start, which adopts and raises both floors.
- The one arm that keeps nothing is `GenesisRoot::Foreign`. A foreign root's cut epoch stays unrecorded until the next resolve of that scope.

## What to decide

Either split the commit so a probe can spend the restrictive half alone, for example a `PendingAdoption::commit_cut_epoch_floor` that takes the `FloorStore` and writes only the cut-epoch raise, or record that a probe is a sighting that spends nothing at all and state that as the rule at the trait definition.

The second option is what #1641 landed, because the probe's whole contract is that a discarded sighting spends nothing, and because splitting the commit adds a second durable write path to the adoption gate. This issue exists to settle which of the two the build wants.

## Acceptance

- The decision is recorded at the `Adopter::probe_read_scope_seed` definition in `crates/engine/src/net/resolve.rs`.
- If the raise is restored, a test proves a probe of a foreign root raises the cut-epoch floor and leaves the sequence floor where it found it.
- If the raise stays dropped, a test proves a probe advances neither floor, and the `GenesisRoot::Foreign` arm carries the reason.

<result># Design study for #1887 — hold a locally authored child in a grafted base

## 1. How the own vault holds such a child today

A create never enters the base. The command seals an op and queues it (`facade.rs:11072`, `sync/staging.rs:81`). The row comes from the overlay, which is recomputed from the queue on every render (`sync/overlay.rs:33`, `facade.rs:10554`). The overlay entry and the queue entry have one lifetime.

After the publish, the drain writes the child into the base itself. It repaints the parent from the children it just published (`drain.rs:5677`, `drain.rs:5846`), and it repaints before it removes the op (`drain.rs:1775`), so no render loses the row. A later merge cannot depart the child either: the publish raises the record's sequence floor, and a folder body at or below that floor is rejected before `merge_folder` sees it (`net/child.rs:349`, `gate/floor.rs:258`).

## 2. Does the grafted path already have this?

A write grant carries the write scope seed at the grant root (`CONTEXT.md:27-28`), so the grantee signs and publishes the parent folder body itself. The blueprint says the sharer only catches up on pin rows (`blueprint/api.md:135`). The grantee's drain therefore runs the same repaint and the same floor raise. The premise in the issue body — that the row dies when the op drains — holds only if the grafted pass repaints under a floor namespace the read legs do not read. The read legs read the sharer-scoped namespace (`facade.rs:6337`); the drain reads one `self.floors` per pass (`drain.rs:5771`), and that namespace is the item lane G6 already reported on #1886.

So the first act of this slice is a test, not a store.

## 3. Options

1. **No new record.** Prove the repaint and the floor with an engine test that drives an upload, a drain and a following pass in a grafted scope. Align the grafted pass's floor namespace with the read legs. Cost: one test file and a small wiring change. Benefit: no persistence surface at all.
2. **A bounded hold set inside the received-share record.** Each bookmark gains a list of node ids this device authored that the sharer's body has not named. No key material, no new key prefix, no new seal kind, no KAT change, no seam change; the hold dies with the bookmark when the grant is cut. The two merge sites already share `GraftedPlane::split`, so the ids pass through the existing `withheld` slice and `merge_folder` stays unchanged.
3. **A new staging prefix and a new `OwnerLocalKind`.** Rejected: a new kind is a frozen registry entry with cross-kind negative vectors (`blueprint/core.md:480`) for data option 2 already carries.

now=$(date -u +%s)
[ $target -le $now ] && target=$((target+86400))

result.output:
- **Bin entry** — one soft-deleted node in the bin index: `nodeId`, `ipnsName`, `kind`, `originParent`, `originName`, `deletedAt`, `scopeId`, and an optional bin-held key. The `ipnsName` is the only remaining route to a record no folder names; `originParent` and `originName` are what a restore puts back.
- **Soft delete** — a delete that unlinks the node and writes a bin entry instead of retiring the record. The owner's bin retention setting chooses it; retention 0 keeps the hard delete.
- **Bin-held key** — the key a soft delete re-keys the doomed subtree under, from the `bin-held-key` edge. It sits outside every scope's derivation, which is the access cut key regression cannot give. Scope-seed shaped: every node of the subtree keys at `readKey(nodeSeed(held, nodeId))`, so the one key the entry carries opens the whole subtree.
- **Restore** — putting a soft-deleted node back into the tree. It re-seals the whole subtree at the destination scope's current epoch, which both returns the node to that scope's grantees and ends the bin-held key's hold on it, then relinks the node and drops the bin entry.
- **Purge** — destroying a soft-deleted node: the reclamation the soft delete deferred, then the bin entry. Irreversible, and refused unless the node is proven unlinked.
- **Bin expiry** — the poll tick queueing a purge for every entry whose `deletedAt` is older than the owner's bin retention, measured on the injected clock. It is what makes retention enforced rather than advisory, and the only thing that frees space under the bin index body's ceiling.
- **Owner capture** — the owner's engine binding an unlink it observes on the poll tick but did not author, and re-keying the node at that adoption. Without it a grantee who unlinks a node in the owner's scope leaves the owner nothing to restore, and keeps the node's read key.

## Sync and refresh

  The retry is idempotent because a duplicate node id is a hard reject at
  encode, so an entry that already landed publishes nothing.
- **A load that carries no member choice takes the soft branch.** A cached
  copy is still the member's choice and still decides the branch; it is the
  documented defaults that fall to the bin. The two errors are not equal: a
  soft delete reclaims nothing and stays reversible, while a hard delete the
  owner did not ask for destroys the node.
- **A child that is a scope root stays hard.** Such a child publishes under a
  name this scope's write seed does not derive. Its subtree is sealed under a
  grantee's own seed, and cutting that grantee is a rotation, not a bin entry.
- **A node the base links more than once unlinks from every one of them.** The
  delete removes the child ref from every folder the base links the node under
  and republishes each under its own plane, under one bin entry whose
  `originParent` names the highest-ranked of those links — the folder a reader
  resolves the node under, and so the folder a restore returns it to — and whose
  `scopeId` names the scope that link resolved onto. The soft branch re-keys the
  ordinary write, so no lazy wave would ever carry it.
- **A descendant scope root is a boundary, not a member.** Its subtree is sealed
  under its own scope's seed, which no grantee of the source scope holds.
- **A re-key that does not land leaves the node linked.** The unlink publishes
  after the re-key, so a failure is retried whole rather than binning a node the
  cut never reached.
- **Every soft delete re-keys, shared scope or not.** The drain carries the
  scope's read and write seeds, never its grant ledger, so it cannot tell a
  scope with live or historical grants from one without. A wrong "unshared"
  verdict is a fail-open disclosure no later pass repairs, and the cost of the
  re-key is the same order as the hard branch's own subtree walk.
- **A create never re-authors over a record that reached the unseal.** The
  replay probe reads a rejection at the unseal stage as published: the record
  verified and cleared both floors, so it is a node the bin re-keyed, and
  re-authoring it under the scope key would resurrect what the bin cut.

content.text:
The blueprint already answers most of this question. So this is a confirmation plus two small choices.

## What the blueprint says now

When a write grantee deletes a file in a shared folder, the grantee's device only removes the file from the folder listing. The owner's device sees that change on its next sync and moves the file into the **owner's** bin. The blueprint calls this "owner capture". The engine has it for the owner's own vault, with tests. The bin belongs only to the owner, and no grant gives access to it. So only the owner can restore or purge the file.

#1901 closed the other path. If the grantee put the file into the grantee's own bin, the owner would lose access to the file.

## Question 1: what can a write grantee do with an existing file?

- **A. Delete means "remove from the shared folder", and the owner's bin gets it (recommended).**
  - Pros: this matches the blueprint and reuses tested code. The owner can undo any delete from the bin.
  - Cons: the owner's device must sync to move the file into the bin. If the owner set bin retention to 0, the delete is final.
  - Restore, purge, and delete of old versions stay refused for the grantee. Those act on the owner's bin and history.
- **B. No delete for a grantee.** A write grantee can add, rename, and edit, but cannot remove files.
  - Pros: the simplest option, with no data loss.
  - Cons: a shared working folder becomes hard to keep clean, and only the owner can remove files.

## Question 2: can a grantee move a file out of the shared folder into their own vault?

- **A. Not in #1886 (recommended).** Moves stay inside the shared folder only. A move out is a copy plus a delete, and it gives the grantee's vault a file that the owner can no longer cut. That needs its own design.
- **B. Allow it in #1886.** This makes #1886 larger and adds a new trust question to the last slice.

## After you answer

Reply with, for example, "1A 2A". I record the decision on #1880 and #1886, and lane G15 builds #1886 to it after #1887 merges. With 1A, #1886 changes the delete path of a grafted pass from "refuse" to "remove the listing entry only". The refusals for restore, purge, and version delete stay.

Lane G17 is complete. It opened draft PR [#1907](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/pull/1907), which closes the new issue #1906. All CI checks are green.

**What #1907 changes:** the web floor store now fails closed. The engine reports `FloorUnreadable` in these cases:

- A floor value is not a non-negative integer. A string, NaN, -1 and 1.5 are examples.
- A stored floor value is corrupt.

Before this fix, such a value read as "no floor" or as 0. The adoption gate on web could then accept a replayed older record.

**One point for you:** JS numbers are exact only up to 2^53 - 1. So the web bridge now refuses any floor above 2^53 - 1, and it does not round the value. The signer of a record chooses its epoch and its sequence. A sharer can therefore publish a larger value, and web then does not adopt that record. Desktop accepts such values. On this point, web and desktop now behave differently. Only the signer of that scope can cause the refusal, so I accept this as fail-closed behavior.

1. #1905 re-review at 05:12Z.
2. #1904 at about 06:15Z.
3. #1907 at about 07:20Z.

<result>The engine reorder did not cause the failure. A race in the test did, and it also fails on the engine from before the reorder. I fixed the test, kept the engine change, and Web E2E Smoke passes on the new head.

**Mechanism.** `ForcedPass::landed()` answers at `manual.settle(...)`, which is before the drain, the mailbox pull (`ShareInbox::pull`) and the received-share status leg (`ReceivedShareStatus::refresh`). The status leg is the only code that writes `received_verdicts`. So `refresh()` in the test returns before the verdict of that pass exists. The test then read `/shared` once and asserted with `toHaveAttribute` for 5 s. Nothing re-read the list, so the page kept the verdict-less read and showed `none`.

- **CI trace (attempt 2):** `refresh()` ran from 18370 to 18458 ms. The pull stored the share, and its mailbox DELETE ran at 18553 ms. The "read again" click ran from 18582 to 18618 ms. The status leg resolved the scope root at 18630 ms, 12 ms after the read. Attempt 1 has the same order: the read at 18002 ms, the mailbox DELETE finished at 18237 ms, and the status leg after that.
- **Why the reorder is not the cause:** `install_unproved_scopes` behaves differently only when a root is in both `proved` and `named` in one walk. For the recipient, both sets are empty: it has no descendant scope, and its one folder publishes at a derived name. The verdict path does not read `unproved_scope_roots` either.
- **Local reproduction, old test:** with the engine from 06ac33f32 (before the reorder), it failed 3 of 8 runs with the same `none`. With 6562f879e it failed 1 of 5.
- **Greptile P1:** the finding is real and the fix is safe. `focus_scope_roots` joins the proved and unproved sets, so a proved root stays a boundary. I kept the engine change and its test. I did not reply in the thread, because the finding was correct.

**Fix: commit `1eaf3f71e`**, "test(web-e2e): re-read the shared list until the forced pass records its verdict".
- I added `SharedPage.readStanding(scope, resolution)` in `/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box-w20-G16/tests/web-e2e/page-objects/shared.page.ts`. It re-reads the list every 250 ms, for at most 10 s, until the standing matches. It does not start another sync pass.

- `/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box-w20-G16/tests/web-e2e/tests/cross-client.spec.ts` had the same race, so I changed it the same way. Its "one nocache refresh" claim still holds.
- I did not change any engine code or engine test.

- `cargo fmt --all --check`: pass.
- `cargo clippy -p cipherbox-engine --all-targets -- -D warnings`: pass.
- Engine lib tests: 1856 passed.
- The web-e2e typecheck, eslint and prettier: pass.
- Local runs of the fixed specs on the 6562f879e engine: 6 of 6, 16 of 16, then 8 of 8 after the CodeRabbit fix.

I merged #1905 into main as `801ea5561`. The post-merge check is green, and I removed the G16 worktree.

- **The smoke failure was a race in the test.** A forced refresh returns before the engine writes the verdict of the received share. The test read the shared list one time only, so the page kept the old read and showed "none".
  - The old engine code fails the same way: 3 of 8 local runs failed.
  - For this recipient, the proved set and the named set are both empty, so the reorder had no effect on this test.
- **The Greptile fix is correct, so I kept it.**
- **The fix is in the tests only.** `contact-grant.spec.ts` and `cross-client.spec.ts` now read the list again every 250 ms, for at most 10 s, until the verdict shows.
- **I merged without a second web review.** After the clean web review, the only new change was in the tests, and the CodeRabbit CLI run on it was clean. Your rule for small, test-side changes lets a clean CLI run replace the second web review.

**Queue:**
- #1904 and #1907 are clean against the new main.
- #1904 also merges with the new main, and the engine compiles after that merge.
- The review of #1904 starts at 06:17Z. #1907 follows at about 07:20Z.

**For you in the morning:**
- **Refresh answers too early.** A forced refresh returns before the engine writes the verdict of a received share. A user who presses refresh can see the old verdict until the next read. The tests now wait for the verdict, but the engine still behaves this way. Tell me if you want an issue for it.
- **Release PR.** Release-please will open a release PR for #1905. Merging it is your decision.

## What happens

A content read of a file below a grafted root fails. `Engine::read_content` and `Engine::file_versions` return `TrustViolation` with the message `adoption gate rejected at stage [unseal]: [seal-open-failed]`. The recipient of a share therefore cannot open, preview or download a file inside a received share, and cannot see its version history.

The error class is also wrong. The record is honest. The engine opens it under the wrong seed, which is a missing capability and not a trust verdict (security rule 6).

## Why

`resolve_versions` in `crates/engine/src/facade.rs` builds its `ChildAdopter` on the vault root scope id and the vault root read seed. The comment there says "subscope reads are a later slice". A file below a grafted root is sealed under the grafted scope's read seed, so the unseal fails. `resolve_head`, `pinned_version`, `read_whole`, `read_version_content` and `version_position` all go through `resolve_versions`.

The same code path reads a file in one of this vault's own interior scopes (a folder the owner granted) under the vault root seed. That case was not measured.

## How it was found

Measured in lane G15 (the write-grant PR for #1886) with the facade `WriteGrantee` harness: the grantee uploads a file below the grafted root, the drain publishes it, and `read_content` on that file returns the `TrustViolation` above. The PR refuses `RestoreVersion` below a grafted root for this reason, because the command reads the version history first.

## Done when

- `resolve_versions` opens a file under the read seed and the floor namespace of the scope the file sits in (`scope_of` over the authored scope roots; `floor_view` for a grafted scope).
- A read below a grafted root and below an own interior scope returns the plaintext, and a test proves each case.
- `RestoreVersion` below a grafted root can then be admitted, if the owner agrees.

# #1911: An epoch-lagged file does not read after a cut. Design study (main d1f05ee30)

## 1. Cause

**The read path has no arm for a lagging record.**
- `resolve_versions` (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs:10677-10696`) resolves the file through `resolve_child` with `ChildAdopter`.
- The adopter runs `floor::check` at `StrictlyNewer` (`net/child.rs:343-351`), then at `AtFloor` (`net/child.rs:205-213`).
- `floor::check` refuses any epoch below the scope read-epoch floor (`gate/floor.rs:291-298`).
- A cut raises that floor at once (`rotation/rotate.rs:363-368`). Every interior node that no write has re-sealed is below the floor "by construction" (`blueprint/engine.md:798`).
- `EngineError::from_gate` reports the refusal as `TrustViolation`. The error class is wrong.

**The sweep is not a durable job.**
- The facade runs `run_sweep` one time per cut, with `SWEEP_MAX_PASSES = 3` (`facade.rs:4624`, `facade.rs:5919-5927`).
- `run_sweep_job`, the idle-cadence job that the blueprint names (`engine.md:819-822`), has no production caller (`rotation/sweep.rs:875`).
- A sweep that fails, or a restart after a cut, leaves files lagging until a write reaches them.

**The measurement probably did not run the sweep.**
- The test `tick` polls only the task list that `boot` took (`tests/write_plane.rs:265-267`, `:314`).
- The sweep that `RotateNow` spawns stays in the scheduler (`testkit/fakes/scheduler.rs:205-207`).
- Thus "20 ticks" does not show that the sweep fails. It shows that reads fail during every sweep window.

## 2. What the floor protects, and where the blueprint applies it

- **On a scope root**, the floor refuses a pre-cut root. Such a root republishes the old override seed, and every revokee who cached that seed can read it. This is a revocation bypass (ADR 0003, "Rejected alternatives"; `engine.md:824-833`).
- **On an interior node**, the stage protects no seed. The record "carries no seed, grant blob or commitment for the stage to protect" (`engine.md:798-800`). The epoch tag attests nothing (ADR 0017 D1).
- **The docs disagree.** Stage 5 applies to "every resolved record" (`CONTEXT.md:74`; `engine.md:206`; #33 D7). But "Epoch lag" says the node is "readable via history links" (`CONTEXT.md:21`). The sweep section names exactly two sanctioned readers below the floor (`engine.md:793-806`). ADR 0012 D2 says: "A third path needs its own decision."
- **Answer to Q1:** No text says that a file must stay refused. No text lets a read admit one.

**Answer to Q2:** The design intends lagging files to be readable. Two parts are missing:
- a read-plane lagging arm, which needs a decision;
- a durable sweep, which is a code defect against `engine.md:819`.

Code applies the floor exactly where the literal gate text applies it.

## 3. Recommended fix: (c), a read-plane lagging arm

**What to do:**
1. When `resolve_child` gets `EpochBelowFloor` for a record with no grant section, anchor on the gated scope root. Take its epoch and its history links, as the drain does at `sync/drain.rs:2197-2230`.
2. Walk the seed back with `seed_at_epoch` (`rotation/reseal.rs:614`).
3. Open the record with `ChildAdopter::open_interior_under` (`net/child.rs:248`).
4. Move `seed_for_lagging` (`drain.rs:506`) out of the drain so that both paths share it. ADR 0012 says that a second copy of a trust check is the defect to avoid.
5. Map the errors:
   - An epoch that the ratchet cannot reach, or an epoch above the root: `ContentUnavailable`.
   - An AAD failure under the seed that the ratchet reached: `TrustViolation`.
6. Wire `run_sweep_job` as the idle job. The blueprint already requires this.

**Trust argument.** The arm holds the four conditions of ADR 0012 D2:
- Stage 3 refuses a grant section before any floor stage runs (`child.rs:112-121`). A scope root is never admitted.
- The replay bar stays (`AtOrAboveFloor`). A record below the per-name sequence floor fails.
- The AAD binds the epoch. A relabelled record opens under no seed.
- The seed comes only from the root that this device gated. The member already holds that key through key regression, so the member learns nothing new and a revokee gains nothing.
- The arm moves no epoch floor.

**Residual.** On a device with no sequence floor for the name, a server can serve an older pre-cut record of the file. The sweep already reads under this same bar, and it then publishes that record forward (`net/rotation.rs:2724-2731`). A read that publishes nothing therefore adds no exposure. The ADR must state whether the arm raises the sequence floor after an unseal, as the sweep does (`rotation.rs:2843-2849`).

**Scope of change:**
- Blast radius: the read path (`resolve_child`), and the focus leg if it opts in.
- No wire format change. No op queue change.
- An ADR is necessary: a third sanctioned reader. Update `engine.md:793-806` ("exactly two" becomes three), `CONTEXT.md` "Adoption gate", and the `Strictness::AtOrAboveFloor` doc.

## 4. Alternatives

- **(a) Parent-named epoch.** `ChildRef` has no epoch field (`core/src/seal/body.rs:78-92`). This needs a wire change and a parent rewrite for each child re-seal. Reject.
- **(b) Reads wait for the sweep.** Reads stay unbounded. A read-only member cannot carry the wave (`engine.md:809`). Offline owners and the retained-window roll-off make lagging files unreadable for good. Reject as the only fix. Wire the durable sweep anyway.
- **(d) Report `ContentUnavailable` and change nothing more.** This fixes the error class only. The file stays unreadable. Reject.

## 5. The share recipient (Q4)

- Today `resolve_versions` reads the owner's vault root scope only ("subscope reads are a later slice", `facade.rs:10666-10669`). A recipient does not reach this path yet.
- When shared reads land, the defect hits the recipient harder. A cut of another member raises the recipient's floor. A read-only recipient cannot sweep or drain, so it waits for the owner.
- The recommended arm covers the recipient. It needs only the current seed and the root's history links, and a current member holds both.

## 6. Tests

1. **Cut, then read.** The test must not drive the sweep. `read_content`, `file_versions` and `read_version_content` return the pre-cut bytes. No floor moves.
2. **Sweep harness.** Take the tasks that the scheduler spawned after the cut, and show that the sweep re-seals the file.
3. A record with a grant section below the floor is refused.
4. A record below the sequence replay bar is refused.
5. A record above the root epoch is `ContentUnavailable`.
6. An epoch that no held link reaches is `ContentUnavailable`, not `TrustViolation`.
7. A record under a relabelled epoch opens under no seed, so it is `TrustViolation`.
8. After a restart, the idle sweep job converges a lagging file.

Two-axis review of the diff between `HEAD` and a fixed point the user supplies:

- **Standards** — does the code conform to this repo's documented coding standards?
- **Spec** — does the code faithfully implement the originating issue / PRD / spec?

Both axes run as **parallel sub-agents** so they don't pollute each other's context, then this skill aggregates their findings.

The issue tracker should have been provided to you — run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` if `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md` is missing.

## Process

### 1. Pin the fixed point

Whatever the user said is the fixed point — a commit SHA, branch name, tag, `main`, `HEAD~5`, etc. If they didn't specify one, ask for it.

Capture the diff command once: `git diff <fixed-point>...HEAD` (three-dot, so the comparison is against the merge-base). Also note the list of commits via `git log <fixed-point>..HEAD --oneline`.

Before going further, confirm the fixed point resolves (`git rev-parse <fixed-point>`) and the diff is non-empty. A bad ref or empty diff should fail here — not inside two parallel sub-agents.

### 2. Identify the spec source

Look for the originating spec, in this order:

1. Issue references in the commit messages (`#123`, `Closes #45`, GitLab `!67`, etc.) — fetch via the workflow in `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`.
2. A path the user passed as an argument.
3. A PRD/spec file under `docs/`, `specs/`, or `.scratch/` matching the branch name or feature.
4. If nothing is found, ask the user where the spec is. If they say there isn't one, the **Spec** sub-agent will skip and report "no spec available".

### 3. Identify the standards sources

Anything in the repo that documents how code should be written, such as `CODING_STANDARDS.md` or `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

On top of whatever the repo documents, the Standards axis always carries the **smell baseline** below — a fixed set of Fowler code smells (_Refactoring_, ch.3) that applies even when a repo documents nothing. Two rules bind it:

- **The repo overrides.** A documented repo standard always wins; where it endorses something the baseline would flag, suppress the smell.
- **Always a judgement call.** Each smell is a labelled heuristic ("possible Feature Envy"), never a hard violation — and, like any standard here, skip anything tooling already enforces.

Each smell reads *what it is* → *how to fix*; match it against the diff:

- **Mysterious Name** — a function, variable, or type whose name doesn't reveal what it does or holds. → rename it; if no honest name comes, the design's murky.
- **Duplicated Code** — the same logic shape appears in more than one hunk or file in the change. → extract the shared shape, call it from both.
- **Feature Envy** — a method that reaches into another object's data more than its own. → move the method onto the data it envies.
- **Data Clumps** — the same few fields or params keep travelling together (a type wanting to be born). → bundle them into one type, pass that.
- **Primitive Obsession** — a primitive or string standing in for a domain concept that deserves its own type. → give the concept its own small type.
- **Repeated Switches** — the same `switch`/`if`-cascade on the same type recurs across the change. → replace with polymorphism, or one map both sites share.
- **Shotgun Surgery** — one logical change forces scattered edits across many files in the diff. → gather what changes together into one module.
- **Divergent Change** — one file or module is edited for several unrelated reasons. → split so each module changes for one reason.
- **Speculative Generality** — abstraction, parameters, or hooks added for needs the spec doesn't have. → delete it; inline back until a real need shows.
- **Message Chains** — long `a.b().c().d()` navigation the caller shouldn't depend on. → hide the walk behind one method on the first object.
- **Middle Man** — a class or function that mostly just delegates onward. → cut it, call the real target direct.
- **Refused Bequest** — a subclass or implementer that ignores or overrides most of what it inherits. → drop the inheritance, use composition.

### 4. Spawn both sub-agents in parallel

Send a single message with two `Agent` tool calls. Use the `general-purpose` subagent for both.

**Standards sub-agent prompt** — include:

- The full diff command and commit list.
- The list of standards-source files you found in step 3, **plus the smell baseline from step 3** pasted in full — the sub-agent has no other access to it.
- The brief: "Report — per file/hunk where relevant — (a) every place the diff violates a documented standard: cite the standard (file + the rule); and (b) any baseline smell you spot: name it and quote the hunk. Distinguish hard violations from judgement calls — documented-standard breaches can be hard, but baseline smells are always judgement calls, and a documented repo standard overrides the baseline. Skip anything tooling enforces. Under 400 words."

**Spec sub-agent prompt** — include:

- The diff command and commit list.
- The path or fetched contents of the spec.
- The brief: "Report: (a) requirements the spec asked for that are missing or partial; (b) behaviour in the diff that wasn't asked for (scope creep); (c) requirements that look implemented but where the implementation looks wrong. Quote the spec line for each finding. Under 400 words."

If the spec is missing, skip the Spec sub-agent and note this in the final report.

### 5. Aggregate

Present the two reports under `## Standards` and `## Spec` headings, verbatim or lightly cleaned. Do **not** merge or rerank findings — the two axes are deliberately separate (see _Why two axes_).

End with a one-line summary: total findings per axis, and the worst issue _within each axis_ (if any). Don't pick a single winner across axes — that's the reranking the separation exists to prevent.

## Why two axes

A change can pass one axis and fail the other:

- Code that follows every standard but implements the wrong thing → **Standards pass, Spec fail.**
- Code that does exactly what the issue asked but breaks the project's conventions → **Spec pass, Standards fail.**

Reporting them separately stops one axis from masking the other.

No documented standard is broken. One terminology problem is close to a hard breach, and seven findings are judgement calls.

7. **Middle Man.** `Engine::vault_root_scope` only calls `held_vault_root_scope`.
8. **Names too close to existing helpers.** `drive` and `run_to_end` are close to `tick` and `poll_tasks_until_parked`.

- **(a) Missing or partial:**
  - The restart test does not cover the vault root, because of #1916. After a restart, the vault-root path of the idle job has no test.
  - A write grantee never runs the sweep. The blueprint says "Runnable by any write-capable client". The brief did not ask for grantee sweeps, but the PR body must state this limit.

- **(c) Implemented, possibly wrong:** the version restore does not add a new version. It moves the old version to the head (`rotate_right`), and the head keeps the old `modified_at`. So the restore changes the order of your version history.

**Summary:** Standards has 8 findings. The worst is the fail-open `receivedShare` default. Spec has 5 findings. The worst is the version restore, which changes the order of your version history.

---

- **B. Keep the version restore for the owner only.** I remove part 2 from #1917, and the refusal stays.

- The sweep and the write wave now pass the verified sequence to the cache write.
- The order does not change: the cache write comes first, and a failed cache write raises no floor.
- **Floor:** if the cache keeps 7 and the pass read 6, the floor goes to 6. This keeps it at or below the cached copy. The raise takes the maximum, so the floor never goes down.

**The situation.** On a device, every record passes the **adoption gate**. For each IPNS name, the gate keeps a **sequence floor**: the highest sequence that the device accepted. The gate refuses a record below that floor, because an older record can be a rollback that an attacker replays. The device also keeps its **last-known-good** copy of each record in the **snapshot cache**. It reads that copy when it is offline.

**The defect (#1913).** A write share raised the sequence floor of a file to 3. The cache still held sequence 2. Offline, the device read the cached copy, and the gate refused it. So the owner could not open the file offline.

**The fix (#1914).** The engine now writes the new bytes to the cache before it raises the floor. So the cache is never below the floor in normal operation.

**The question.** #1914 also changed what the user sees when a cached copy is below the floor. Before, the engine reported a **trust violation**. Now it reports "content unavailable". Your security rule 6 says that a gate failure is always a trust violation and never "only stale". So this change breaks the rule, and the blueprint has no exception for it.

After the fix, a cached copy below the floor occurs only in two cases:
- The cache is corrupt, or someone put a record into it.
- A rare timing race occurs between two passes. The resolve push makes this race narrower.

**The two choices:**
- **A. Keep the rule.** The engine reports a trust violation again. In the rare race, an offline read shows a trust error until the next online read repairs the cache.
- **B. Change the rule.** An ADR adds an exception: a stale copy of your own record below the floor is "content unavailable". The user sees a milder message, but the gate law gets weaker.

I recommend **A**.

content.text:
The difference is small in the web app and larger on desktop.

**Web app:**
- A failed download or open shows one error line above the file list. The line is the raw engine message. For a trust violation it starts with "trust violation: adoption gate rejected…". For "content unavailable" it gives the unavailability reason.
- The web app does not branch on the error class for a read. The same bar shows both errors, and neither one retries automatically.
- The web app also has a separate warning area for trust violations (`notification.store.ts`). The engine fills it only from its refresh legs and from the bin index, not from a content read. So an offline read in the race window does not show a standing warning.

**Desktop (FUSE mount):**
- A **trust violation** becomes `EIO` on macOS and Linux (`STATUS_DATA_ERROR` on Windows). An application treats this as a hard I/O error: "the file is damaged". The mount does not retry, and it does not render the file.
- **Content unavailable** becomes `EAGAIN`. An application treats this as "try again later". Some applications retry by themselves.

**What this means for option A:** in the rare race, an offline desktop user gets a hard I/O error on a file that is not damaged. The error clears when the device is online again and the next read repairs the cache. A web user sees an error line that says "trust violation" and not "offline".

I still recommend option A:
- After the resolve push, the race needs two passes that overlap on one name while the device is offline, so it is rare.
- In the other case (a corrupt cache or a planted record), the hard error is correct.
- The desktop `EIO` is the price of the strict law. It does not cause a lockout or data loss.

If you choose A, I put it in the #1914 resolve brief and correct #1913, which asked for the downgrade.

CodeRabbit refused the #1914 request again because of the rate limit. The next slot opens at about 13:13Z. Greptile reviewed the new head and gave 4/5 with a new P1. The P1 is the same race that the spec review found:

> The sequence check and cache write are separate operations. If two passes for the same name both read the older cached value, the newer pass can write first and the older pass can then overwrite it with a lower sequence. […] This needs per-name serialization or an atomic conditional cache operation.

This changes my advice on the downgrade question. The re-read before the put only makes the race window smaller. The race can still occur. With option A, the race gives a desktop user a hard `EIO` error on a file that is not damaged.

**A better fix needs no seam change:** the engine takes an in-memory lock for each name around the sequence of cache read, compare and put. The tick, the sweep and the write wave all go through the same engine, so one lock map in memory serializes them. The race then cannot occur. The only remaining case is a corrupt or planted cache, and for that case a trust violation is correct.

So I recommend:
- **A:** keep the rule, which means you keep `TrustViolation`.
- **The per-name lock:** add it in the same resolve push, so the race goes away completely.

- **A read-only audit:** it searches the whole engine for other places that read rule 6 wrongly.

READ-ONLY audit of FSM1/cipher-box main. No file edits, no git writes, no GitHub posts. Work in `/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box` (run `git fetch -q origin` and read `origin/main` with `git show origin/main:<path>` or `git grep ... origin/main`; do not switch branches). Prefix gh commands with `env -u GITHUB_TOKEN`.

## The rule
AGENTS.md security rule 6: "Every resolved record passes the adoption gate; a failure is a fail-closed trust violation, never mere staleness." `CONTEXT.md` "Adoption gate" and `blueprint/engine.md` ("A gate failure is never mere staleness") say the same. The ONLY accepted exception is ADR 0021 (FSM1/cipher-box-next `decisions/0021-*.md`, accepted 2026-09-19): a lagging interior record whose epoch the scope root's ratchet does not reach is reported unreachable (`ContentUnavailable`). Read `CONTEXT.md` "Adoption gate" on main for the exact exception text.

## The misreading we found
Several lane agents cited rule 6 in REVERSE, as "a missing capability is not a trust verdict" or "stale, not a verdict on anyone (rule 6)", to justify mapping a gate rejection to `ContentUnavailable` / `Unavailable`. The owner decided on 2026-09-19 that a gate rejection is always a `TrustViolation` (open PR #1914 removes one such downgrade in `net/child.rs`).

## Task
1. Find every place on origin/main where the engine (crates/engine, crates/fuse, crates/wasm, crates/desktop-*, apps/desktop/src-tauri) or a host maps a `GateError::Rejected` / a `RejectionReason` / a gate verdict to something other than a trust violation (e.g. `ContentUnavailable`, `Unavailable`, `Stale`, `NotFound`, `None`, a silent skip, a retry, `EAGAIN`), OR cites "rule 6"/"security rule 6" in a comment. `git grep -n "rule 6" origin/main`, grep `Rejected(`, `from_gate`, `SequenceNotNewer`, `EpochBelowFloor`, `ContentUnavailable`, `Unavailable`, `TrustViolation`, `bin_load_is_a_verdict`, `is_a_verdict`, `Stale {`.
2. For each hit classify:
   - CORRECT: a real non-gate availability failure (a seam/network error, no record at all, no seed held so nothing was resolved), or the ADR 0021 exception, or a correct TrustViolation.
   - MISREAD: a gate REJECTION reported as availability/staleness, or a comment that states rule 6 in reverse.
   - UNCLEAR: explain.
   Also check the merged PRs of today for this pattern: #1912 ("a node below no known scope root is ContentUnavailable" — is anything gated there?), #1905, #1910, #1907 (web floor store `FloorUnreadable`), and the text of issues #1909, #1911, #1913, #1916 (issue text that restates rule 6 in reverse).
3. For every MISREAD: file:function, the exact code/comment, what the user sees now (web error line / desktop errno EIO vs EAGAIN), and the correct mapping.
4. Also list OTHER repercussions of the option-A decision: places where a trust violation now reaches a user for a benign cause (e.g. a stale own cache, a race, a restart), a UI that treats `trustViolation` differently (web `notification.store.ts` warning surface, desktop `emit_trust_violation`, FUSE `EIO`/`STATUS_DATA_ERROR`), and any retry/backoff logic that treats the two classes differently.

## Report
In ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English, under 700 words: a table of MISREAD items (file:function, code, user-visible effect, correct mapping), the UNCLEAR items, the issue texts that restate rule 6 in reverse, and the other repercussions. List CORRECT items only as a count by category.

I recorded option A in memory, and the resolve agent for #1914 now has it. Before the 13:13Z slot, it removes the downgrade and adds the per-name lock. It also fixes the other findings.

**Consequences that I know now:**
- **Desktop:** a trust violation is a hard `EIO` (on Windows, `STATUS_DATA_ERROR`). The mount does not retry it. So every benign cause that still reaches the gate becomes a hard error for the user. The audit sorts each place into one of three classes:

- **Misread:** a gate rejection that the engine reports as availability.

The drain emits no trust event. The user sees a stalled write. | Emit a trust violation and use a halt that names the verdict, as `report_author_refusal` does. |
| 5 | `crates/engine/src/facade.rs` `focus_scope_roots` doc | "availability laundered into a trust verdict (security rule 6)" | Comment only. The code is correct. | Rule 6 forbids the opposite direction. Remove the rule 6 citation. |

No. Item 3 is not about `focus.rs`. Item 1 is the `focus.rs` point, and it is decided: the ADR 0021 lane fixes it.

Item 3 is about the **status of a received share**. This is the standing that a recipient sees on each share row in "Shared with me".

**How it works now.** A recipient's engine checks each received share again from time to time. It reads the scope root at the share's name, and the adoption gate checks that record. Then the engine puts the share into one of four classes (`ResolutionClass` in `grants/revocation.rs`). The blueprint requires these four ("revocation is discovered, not delivered"):

| Class | Meaning | What the row shows |
|---|---|---|
| `Granted` | A current record from the sharer still holds your grant blob. | granted |
| `RevocationSignal` | A current record has no blob for you. The sharer revoked the share. | revoked |
| `Unresolvable` | The name did not resolve. | unknown or stale |
| `EpochLag` | A current record is at an older epoch, and the sweep is pending. | stale, wait |

**The problem.** Say that someone serves an **older** record of the share: a rollback, or a replayed record from before a cut. The gate refuses it, because its sequence is below the floor. The engine then puts the share into `Unresolvable`, as if the name only failed to resolve. The code even calls it "a replay, not a verdict". So the user sees "unknown or stale" and gets no warning, although an attack on this share is possible. Rule 6 forbids exactly that.

**Why this is a decision for you.** The four classes have no class for "the gate refused a record". So the fix can go one of two ways:

- **A. Add a fifth class, for example `TrustViolation`.** The share row itself shows a trust warning. This is the most direct result for the user. But it changes the classifier that the blueprint defines, so it needs a short ADR, and the web and desktop share rows need a new state.
- **B. Keep the four classes, and also emit a trust-violation event.** The row still shows "unknown or stale". The warning goes to the warning area of the web (the toast) and to the desktop tray. That obeys rule 6, and it needs no ADR and no new UI state. But the warning is not on the share row.

I recommend **B**, because the user still gets the trust warning and the change is smaller.

If you want the warning directly on the share row, choose A. Then I write the ADR first, and the lane builds the class after you accept it.

The diff shown in the skill preamble was empty because that preamble ran in the main checkout. This review used the lane worktree `/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box-w20-G22` and the diff `origin/main...HEAD`.

## Candidates considered and rejected

1. **An old vault pointer laundered through the catch-up or the cut.** Rejected. `open_repoint` checks the owner signature. The code refuses a standing re-point that names a root other than the session root. `minReadEpoch` is the only field that changes, and it only goes up. `writeEpoch`, `prevRoot` and `scopeId` carry over, so nothing rolls back.
2. **`minReadEpoch` raised from attacker data.** Rejected. The value comes from one of two places:
   - in the cut, the epoch this device just published;
   - in the catch-up, the local durable floor, which rises only after a gated adopt of an owner-signed root.
3. **An older pointer overwrites a newer one because the CAS bar is bypassed.** Rejected. A publish over a replayed lower sequence loses record selection on honest endpoints and reports `LostRace` or `Unconfirmed`. The attack works only if the attacker controls every endpoint, and then it is withholding, which is DoS and out of scope.
4. **The `landed` resume skips the gate.** Rejected. The value comes only from this device's own confirmed root publish and lives for one `rotate_now` call.
5. **The floor is raised past the vault pointer.** Rejected. The order is root publish, then vouch, then floor raise and sweep. A vouch that fails leaves the floor where it was.
6. **Entropy, nonces, key exposure and logging.** Rejected. The nonce comes through the injected `Entropy` seam. The pointer read key is `SecretBytes`. Nothing is logged.
7. **Trust vs availability.** Not a vulnerability. An `Absent` vault pointer maps to `Rejected`, which fails closed. An attacker who returns 404 everywhere can only stall a cut, which is DoS.</result>

<result>PR #1919 is open as a draft and all CI checks pass. The fix works: after a read cut of the vault root, the device and a second device start again. One narrow lockout remains, and only an ADR can close it.

**PR:** https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/pull/1919 (draft). Branch `fix/1916-root-read-cut-repoints`, head `c7eb783be`, one unsigned commit with no attribution trailer. The body has a bare `Closes #1916.`, and GitHub shows #1916 as the closing reference.

**CI (one wait):** all checks are success. That includes Rust fmt + clippy, workspace tests, engine simulation tests, Core KATs (native and WASM), adapter tests (Windows and macOS), Client Browser Suite, Web Engine WASM, Web E2E Smoke, Contract Suite, Lint, Tracker Refs and the PR title check. The API, Desktop and Web typecheck jobs were skipped by change detection. No re-run was necessary.

**What was wrong:** the cut raised the durable read floor, but the vault pointer still vouched the old epoch. The cold-start check then refused the device (`vouched 1 below durable floor 2`). A second device also failed, on its second start, because its first start adopted the cut root and raised its own floor. The issue text says the second device starts. It does, but only one time.

**Order chosen and why:**
1. Publish the root at the new epoch.
2. Vouch the new epoch at the vault pointer. The owner signs the same re-point with only `minReadEpoch` raised, and the vouch refuses a re-point that names another root.
3. Raise the durable floor.
4. Enqueue the lazy wave.

- **Why the root goes first:** if the vouch goes first and the root publish fails, every device seeds a floor above the only root. The owner then cannot cut again, so every device is bricked.
- **Why the vouch goes before the floor:** if the floor goes first and the vouch fails, this device is locked out. That is the bug in #1916.
- **Retry:** a retry finishes the cut that already landed and does not cut again. A new cut would first adopt the landed root, and that raises the floor past a vault pointer that did not move.
- **Cold-start catch-up:** when a start adopts the root above the vouched epoch, it vouches that epoch before the loops start. If this fails, it sends `RenewalFailed` with the vault-pointer name.
- **Refusal:** a cut of the vault root with no vault-pointer signer is refused before anything is minted.
- **Unchanged:** `repoint_regression`, the seams, the wire format and the durable record kinds do not change.

**Path table:**

| Path | Result |
| --- | --- |
| RotateNow at the vault root | Fixed |
| Scope-exit cut | Cannot name the vault root; it only holds descendant roots |
| Revoke at the root, read or full, with or without the write arm | Refused before any rotation; the vault root has no grants |
| Downgrade at the root | Refused before any rotation |
| Grant at the root | Refused (`UnsupportedTarget`) |
| Grant of a child folder | Parent root republishes at the same epoch |
| Write wave at the root | Carries the durable floor as `minReadEpoch`; the facade cannot reach it |
| Sweep and drain wave | Re-seal interior nodes only |

**Tests:** I added 9 tests in a new section of `crates/engine/tests/mount_convergence.rs`:
- The same device restarts after the cut. This test failed before the fix.
- A second device starts two times.
- The vouch never lands: the device still starts, the next start vouches the epoch, and the cut happens one time only.
- The root never lands: the vault pointer does not change.
- A failed catch-up sends its event.
- Each of the two vouch refusals fires.
- Grant, revoke and downgrade at the root, followed by a restart.

All 16 tests in the file pass, and the full engine suite passes. Of 8 mutations, 8 were killed.

**UI reachability:** only `packages/client` exposes `rotateNow`. Nothing in `apps/web` or `apps/desktop` calls it, so no user can do this cut from the product today. The severity is low.

**Reviews (all run in the foreground):**
- **simplify:** applied a shared `complete_cut`, a `From<PointerPublishFailure>`, the new root refusal, the failure event and shorter comments. I rejected the shared vouch body because the two bars are different.
- **code-review:** added tests for the two refusals. I renamed the types to `VaultPointerVoucher` and `VouchedRoot`, because the blueprint uses "vault anchor" for the root scope.
- **security-review:** no finding at confidence 8 or above.
- **crypto-privacy reviewer and the independent reviewer:**
  - They found that the catch-up comment wrongly said the next start runs it again. I fixed the comment.
  - I changed the missing-signer refusal to Unavailable.
  - I kept the stale-record re-sign finding at Low. Records that name one root differ only in `minReadEpoch`, and the vouch only raises it. To fork the record, an attacker must control every endpoint.

All summaries are in `/tmp/w19/lane-G22/review.md`. I did not run the CodeRabbit CLI at any time.

**Decision for you — the lockout that remains:**
- **When it happens:** the vault-pointer PUT fails while record reads work, for longer than the retry bound. The same happens when a root publish comes back unconfirmed but did land. In both cases the running session adopts the cut root and raises its floor. The next start of that device is then refused, until another owner device starts and vouches the epoch. A user with one device stays locked.
- **Why I did not close it:** the crypto-privacy reviewer confirmed that closing it needs a change to the floor law or to the cold-seed check. That is a trust-boundary change and needs an ADR, so I stopped there.
- **Partial option without an ADR:** a catch-up in the running tick would make the window smaller. It would also keep the owner signing key in the tick, so I did not add it.

I filed no follow-up issue and made no issue edits. The PR stays draft; I did not mark it ready or merge it. No timer or background command is running.</result>

Lane G22 opened draft PR [#1919](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/pull/1919), which closes #1916. All CI checks pass, and the lane did not run the CLI.

**The fix:** a read cut of the vault root now runs in this order:
1. Publish the root at the new epoch.
2. The owner signs the vault pointer again with the new `minReadEpoch`. This step is called the vouch.
3. Raise the durable floor.
4. Start the sweep.

**Why this order:**
- If the vouch comes before the root publish and the publish fails, every device gets a floor above the only root. That is a lockout on all devices.
- If the floor comes before the vouch and the vouch fails, this device is locked out. That is the bug in #1916.

**Other changes:**
- A retry finishes a cut that already landed, and it does not cut again.
- If a start finds the root above the vouched epoch, it vouches that epoch before the loops start.
- Revoke, downgrade and grant at the vault root are refused before any rotation.
- The lane found one more case: a second device also failed, on its second start.
- There are 9 new tests with restarts, and all 8 mutations were caught.

**Severity:** low. `rotateNow` exists only in `packages/client`. Nothing in the web app or the desktop app calls it.

**Decision for you: one narrow lockout remains.**
- **When it happens:** the vault-pointer publish fails for longer than the retry limit while reads still work. It also happens when a root publish reports "unconfirmed" but did land. In both cases, the running session adopts the cut root and raises its floor. The next start of that device is refused until another device of the owner starts and vouches the epoch. So a user with one device stays locked out.
- **Why the lane stopped there:** a full fix changes the floor law or the cold-start check. That is a change at the trust boundary, so it needs an ADR.

My recommendation:
- Merge #1919 as it is. It removes the lockout that can occur in normal use.
- File the remaining case as a new issue, `post-cutover`, with the note "needs an ADR".
- Write the ADR when a UI starts to offer the root cut. No user can reach this path now.

Tell me if you agree. Then I file the issue.

cat > /tmp/w19/i-lockout.md <<'EOF'
## Problem

After a read cut of the vault root, one device can still be locked out at its next cold start. PR #1919 closes the common case: the cut now publishes the root, vouches the new epoch at the vault pointer (`minReadEpoch`), and only then raises the durable floor. One narrow case stays open.

The lockout occurs in these two conditions:

- The vault-pointer publish fails for longer than the retry bound, while record reads still work.
- A root publish reports "unconfirmed" but did land.

In both conditions, the running session adopts the cut root at the new epoch and raises its durable read-epoch floor. The vault pointer still vouches the old `minReadEpoch`. At the next cold start of that device, `repoint_regression` (`crates/engine/src/gate/floor.rs`) refuses the start: `read-epoch floor regression: vouched N below durable floor N+1`.

The device stays locked out until another device of the owner starts and vouches the epoch (the cold-start catch-up in PR #1919). A user with one device stays locked out.

## Severity

Low now. Only `packages/client` exposes `rotateNow`. No code in `apps/web` or `apps/desktop` calls it, so no user can start a read cut of the vault root from the product. The severity changes when a UI offers the cut.

## Why this needs an ADR

The crypto-privacy review on PR #1919 found that a full fix changes the floor law or the cold-start check. `repoint_regression` is the rollback guard of the cold-start anchor. A change to it is a trust-boundary change, so it needs an ADR in FSM1/cipher-box-next, and the owner must accept it before the code changes.

A partial fix is possible without an ADR: a vouch catch-up in the running tick makes the window smaller. It keeps the owner signing key in the tick, so PR #1919 did not add it. The ADR should decide on it too.

## Done when

- An accepted ADR states how a device that raised its own floor by its own cut starts when the vault pointer did not move, without a weaker rollback guard.
- The engine follows the ADR, and a restart test covers each of the two conditions above with one device only.

## Relates to

- #1916, which PR #1919 closes.
- The lane G22 review record for PR #1919.
EOF

The idle job then recorded the scope as converged at its epoch and skipped it until the epoch increased. If the writer that won the race did not repair the index, the missing child-scope entry stayed missing.

**Fix.** The fix is in `crates/engine/src/rotation/sweep.rs`, where the rule lives:
- A new field, `SweepOutcome::index_repair_lost_race`, is set when the repair loses the CAS.
- `worth_another_pass()` counts that field. The idle job therefore keeps the scope due, and a later round derives the index again and publishes it.
- The value from the last pass is kept across passes, like the other re-derived buckets.
- `run_sweep` also runs the pass again for the same reason.

34-- **Envelope** — the published plaintext wrapper of a node: format version, node id, epoch tag, the sealed bodies, and (at scope roots only) the grant section. Kind-uniform: whether a node is a file or a folder is sealed inside the read-body.
35-- **Write-body** — the sealed write-plane payload, present only at scope roots: the grant ledger plus the write-plane history link. Interior nodes publish none; all their write material is derived.
36-- **Blinded tag** — the opaque per-pair label a grant blob is keyed by, derived from an owner–recipient shared secret and the scope root's name. Observers learn only blob count; the recipient self-locates their blob.

Writers re-wrap blobs for the recorded set during re-seals but cannot change the set; grant changes are owner-only. A re-seal takes every recipient encryption key off the grant-set commitment, never off a row, so a relabelled row misdirects nothing; the row's `recipientIdentityPk` is a label no commitment field covers, and a re-mint drops it unless the row's own owner signature attests it. Each row carries an owner signature over `{ipnsName, recipientEncPk, recipientIdentityPk, tag}`. That signature is transferable: a co-writer can extract it and prove to anyone holding the owner's contact code that a given identity is a grantee of this scope root. Grant membership is non-deniable **within the grant set**: a co-writer reads the ledger, and any grantee of the scope unmasks the commitment's recipients under the scope `pointerReadKey`. content.text:
## Point 1 — the forgery window now reaches readers

**What the forgery window is.** `CONTEXT.md` names it as an accepted residual. When the owner revokes a write grant, the engine rotates the names in a wave. Until the wave reaches a name, the revoked writer still holds the old seed for that name and can seal a plausible record at the old epoch and publish it at the old name. The epoch label attests nothing about who sealed the body (ADR 0017). The bound is the wave for a write grantee, and about one pointer-consult interval for a read-only member.

**What changed.** Before #1921, a member's read refused a record below the read-epoch floor. Only the sweep and the drain opened such a record. Now the read arm opens it too, so a forged record from that window can render to the user as file content.

**Why this is not a new key exposure.** The revoked writer gets nothing new. The arm gives no seed to anyone, and the seed comes only from the root that this device gated. The change is in reach: the forged bytes now reach the screen of a reader directly, and not only through the sweep that would republish them.

**How wide it is.** The wave bounds it, as `CONTEXT.md` states. The sweep already republishes such a record forward, so the same bytes would reach the reader a little later in any case.

**What ADR 0021 says today.** Its trust argument covers the seed, a relabelled record, the replay bar and the revocation boundary. Its residual E1 covers only the first read on a device that has no sequence floor for the name. It does not name the forgery window.

**Your choices:**
- **A. Add a residual E2 to ADR 0021.** One paragraph: the arm brings the forgery window to the read path, the wave bounds it, and the sweep already carries the same bytes. This is a docs PR, and it changes no code. I recommend A.
- **B. Bound it in code.** The reader would refuse a lagging record whose sequence is above the sequence that the parent folder named before the cut. That needs a new decision and more state, and it can refuse honest records. I do not recommend B now.

## Point 2 — a second device after a cut of the vault root

**What the lane saw.** In a test, a second device of the same owner does a cold start after the first device cut the vault root. At that moment the second device holds no read seed for the root scope. It gets one on its first tick.
